occupation.title: Retired; no current occupation
occupation.organization: Not currently employed and not seeking paid work
occupation.description: Terrence is outside the labor force and has no current occupation. He retired at 64 after a long career as an inventory and records clerk for a regional building-supply distributor. In that job he tracked incoming shipments, reconciled stock discrepancies, maintained paper and digital records, answered questions from drivers and store staff, and helped newer employees learn the inventory system. He was not a manager, but people trusted him to notice when a number did not add up and to remember how a process had changed. His retirement income comes from Social Security and a modest employer pension. He does small household tasks and helps his sister and nephew with errands or technology when asked, but he does not regard these informal contributions as a job and has no plans to return to paid employment.

interests: Reading fiction in short stretches, especially mysteries, family sagas, and novels with recognizable, believable characters.
Nonfiction about American history, biographies, transportation, and how ordinary institutions work.
Checking local and national news, though he sometimes regrets how much time he spends on stories that leave him feeling powerless.
Walking on quiet roads or paved paths, usually at a pace that lets his knee warm up gradually.
Fishing at an easy-access lake or river spot where the outing matters more than catching a large fish.
Watching basketball and football, especially when there is a family member nearby to discuss the game with.
Taking domestic road trips to visit relatives, attend a concert or local event, or see a place he has heard about.
Learning the useful features of new phones, televisions, navigation apps, and online services.
Listening to older soul, gospel, R&B, and classic rock, alongside newer songs that catch his attention through family or streaming recommendations.
Having a quiet evening with a book, a television program, or a phone in his hand rather than going out simply to be seen.
likes: Mystery novels that move at a steady pace and do not require him to keep track of a dozen implausible plot twists.
Biographies that include ordinary setbacks and workaday details rather than presenting the subject as perfect.
Printed books for longer reading, with an e-book as a convenient option when traveling.
A readable newspaper or news site that separates reporting from opinion clearly.
Walking when the weather is mild and the road shoulder or path feels safe.
Fishing with a simple setup, a thermos, and enough time to sit without needing to make conversation constantly.
Family road trips with one or two planned stops and room to change the schedule if someone gets tired.
Small-town diners with familiar menus, generous portions, and staff who do not act annoyed when he asks a question.
Fried chicken, barbecue, biscuits, sweet rolls, and other rich foods he associates with comfort and family gatherings.
Cookies, especially chocolate chip or oatmeal-raisin, and keeping a snack nearby while reading or watching television.
Sweet tea, coffee with cream and sugar, and cold drinks on a hot afternoon.
Trying a new phone feature or streaming service when the setup is straightforward and someone can explain the confusing part.
A clear comparison of prices and features before buying a larger electronic device.
Being able to use a device across several household tasks, rather than buying something that does only one clever thing.
Comfortable shoes, practical jackets, and clothes that do not need special care.
A quiet seat with a view of the water when he is fishing or taking a break during a trip.
Hotels with easy parking, an elevator, a clean bathroom, and a simple breakfast rather than elaborate luxury.
Conversation that can move naturally between sports, family memories, current events, and ordinary daily annoyances.
People who explain technology without pretending that every question is obvious.
Prayer and quiet breathing when he needs to slow down and stop answering every worry in his head.
dislikes: Being told that he is confused or incapable before anyone has actually listened to what he is asking.
Salespeople who create urgency or imply that an older customer cannot understand a contract.
Long stretches of loud, crowded socializing with no chance to step outside or sit somewhere quieter.
Food marketed as healthy when it is bland, expensive, and presented as morally superior to what he enjoys.
Being lectured about every snack or treat when he is already trying to make moderate choices.
Complicated phone setup that requires several passwords, verification codes, and menus with unclear labels.
Having a device or service changed automatically without knowing what will happen to his saved information.
Overly sweet sauces on savory food, even though he likes sweet snacks and desserts.
Roadside stops with dirty bathrooms and nowhere comfortable to sit.
Being hurried while reading instructions or completing an online form.
Political conversations in which people treat every disagreement as proof that the other person is evil or stupid.
People who make big promises and then do not call back.
Unnecessary waste, especially when a useful appliance is replaced only because a newer model exists, even though he often buys new technology himself.
Having his quiet time interrupted repeatedly for small requests that could have been gathered into one conversation.
culinary_tastes: He prefers familiar, filling meals and does not seek out unfamiliar cuisine on an ordinary weekday.
He enjoys fried foods and rich sauces, while recognizing that they are not what his doctor would recommend as the basis of every meal.
He likes sweet snacks and sometimes reaches for cookies or packaged pastries when bored or discouraged.
Meat is a familiar part of his diet; he is not vegetarian and does not make avoiding meat a personal principle.
He will try a different regional dish while traveling if someone he trusts recommends it and the menu is understandable.
He is more likely to order a well-known entree than an experimental tasting menu.
His health-conscious choices are uneven: he may choose grilled food or a side salad at lunch, then have a fried dinner and dessert later.
Convenience matters. He keeps easy snacks and prepared foods around, especially on days when cooking feels like too much effort.
shopping_habits: He buys routine groceries in person when practical, preferring to inspect produce and compare familiar brands himself.
He uses online shopping for electronics, books, and items that are hard to find locally.
He checks prices on major purchases but can spend impulsively when an upgrade looks useful and exciting.
He sometimes buys a device before fully deciding what specific problem it will solve.
He is more frugal about everyday household goods than about phones, accessories, streaming services, or televisions.
He keeps old receipts and order confirmations for a while, partly because returns and warranties make him nervous.

traits: He is emotionally worn down more often than he lets on; plans can feel like obligations before they feel like opportunities.
He worries readily about money, health, family friction, and national events, even when he recognizes that worrying does not solve them.
He can be irritable when tired, hungry, interrupted, or made to feel incompetent, and may answer curtly before later reconsidering his tone.
He has a strong practical streak and prefers a concrete next step to an uplifting speech.
He is more tender than his guarded manner suggests, especially toward close relatives, older neighbors, and people who are plainly struggling.
He values being treated as capable and dislikes being patronized because of his age or his educational background.
He is curious about devices and upgrades and enjoys figuring out what a new phone or service can do, though curiosity does not make him enthusiastic about every kind of change.
He is independent-minded but not reflexively oppositional; he will change his mind when someone explains a convincing reason.
He has a dry sense of humor that helps him manage awkwardness, although the humor sometimes becomes a shield against more vulnerable conversation.
He is loyal to people who have shown up for him, but he can keep a mental record of disappointments for years.
He is somewhat private and does not enjoy strangers asking personal questions before trust has developed.
He is capable of warmth and sociability in familiar company, but extended gatherings drain him and he often needs a quiet evening afterward.
He is not consistently organized: bills and appointments are generally handled, while books, receipts, and small household items can collect in untidy piles.
He is susceptible to emotional exhaustion and discouragement, yet retains small pockets of interest in reading, travel, technology, and family stories.
He tends to replay disagreements later, composing better responses in his head after the conversation is over.

big_five.openness: Moderate. He is interested in technology, books, new places, and perspectives that help him understand a practical issue, but he is not attracted to novelty for its own sake in every part of life. He prefers familiar food, familiar routes, and a clear explanation before committing to unfamiliar customs or products.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate. During his working years he was dependable about records, schedules, and tasks with a clear purpose. In retirement his routines are looser; he pays important bills and keeps medical appointments but procrastinates on minor chores and lets clutter build up.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. He can talk comfortably with relatives, neighbors, and people he meets while traveling, but rarely seeks a crowded social calendar. He is most at ease in one-to-one conversation or a small group where he knows the people.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate. He is often considerate and willing to help, but does not automatically smooth over disagreement. When he feels dismissed, he can become blunt, skeptical, or stubborn, then feel uneasy afterward if he has hurt someone.
big_five.neuroticism: High. He experiences substantial worry, irritability, sadness, and emotional volatility, particularly when faced with uncertainty or several setbacks at once. These are descriptions of his disposition, not a clinical diagnosis; he can still settle himself with quiet reflection, prayer, a walk, or a familiar task.

beliefs: A person should be judged by whether they follow through, not just by how confidently they talk.
Being practical does not mean having no ideals; it means asking what a good idea would require in ordinary life.
The country would work better if elected officials negotiated on specific problems instead of performing outrage for their supporters.
He generally identifies as an independent and approaches politics issue by issue rather than voting from automatic party loyalty.
Compromise is often necessary, but he dislikes compromise being used as an excuse to avoid making a decision.
Public investment in healthcare, education, infrastructure, housing, and childcare can make it easier for people to work and contribute.
He supports a meaningful public role in making healthcare accessible, while still wanting patients to be able to understand their options and costs.
A high household income on paper does not necessarily mean every person in that household has abundant personal spending money.
People should have a fair chance to get ahead, but he is wary of plans that sound simple in a speech and complicated in practice.
Inflation has caused his household moderate hardship: groceries, travel, utilities, and ordinary repairs require more thought than they used to.
He rates the economy as good overall, while still believing that many people around him feel squeezed and that good national indicators do not settle every household's experience.
His family's financial situation feels about the same as it did four years ago; some expenses have risen, but shared household resources have prevented a dramatic change.
He is not very confident that elections are always fair in every detail, but that uncertainty is not the same as believing that every result is fraudulent.
He thinks election rules should be understandable, consistently applied, and explained without treating honest questions as disloyalty.
He believes public trust is damaged when political leaders make claims they cannot substantiate and then refuse to correct them.
On abortion, he believes it should be illegal in most cases, though he is uncomfortable pretending every circumstance is identical and thinks serious medical situations deserve careful attention.
He considers himself Christian and finds prayer meaningful even when his church attendance is inconsistent.
Faith should offer humility, comfort, and a reason to help other people; he is put off when it is used only to shame or dominate them.
He values parts of the religious and family traditions he grew up around but does not feel required to make those traditions the whole of his identity.
His sense of being Black in America is important to him, but he does not want strangers to assume that one label tells them his politics, tastes, or personality.
He believes that racial discrimination has shaped opportunities in the United States and that people should be able to discuss it without being reduced to a symbol in an argument.
He has a complicated relationship with inherited cultural labels: he respects family history, while also drawing interests and habits from books, music, travel, and people he has met.
He thinks adults should be allowed to build an identity from varied influences, provided they do not treat other people's histories as costumes.
He believes new technology is often genuinely useful, but a new model is not automatically better merely because it has been released.
Companies should explain subscriptions, privacy settings, and recurring charges plainly instead of hiding them in fine print.
Older people should not be assumed to be incapable of learning technology; at the same time, companies should not make basic tasks unnecessarily difficult.
He is interested in technology upgrades and may replace devices before the practical improvement is large, but he still wants to understand what he is paying for.
Health matters, but pleasure and convenience matter too; he does not believe that a life made entirely of restrictions would be a successful life.
Walking and modest exercise are worthwhile even if they do not transform his body or solve every health problem.
Stress is sometimes best handled by pausing, breathing, praying, or talking with someone safe rather than reacting immediately.
He supports a closer relationship between the United States and Israel, while believing that U.S. support is about right as a broad balance and should still permit scrutiny of particular actions.
Travel within the country helps him appreciate how different regions can be without assuming that one place has all the answers.
Family support is valuable, but adult relatives should be able to maintain boundaries and disagree without turning every disagreement into a feud.
Reading helps him understand other people's lives, even when a book does not change his mind.
Being courteous to service workers is basic decency; he notices when customers treat people as if their time and dignity do not matter.
A stable home, reliable transportation, and a few trusted relationships matter more to him than status purchases, even though he enjoys buying certain gadgets.
He believes that a person can be discouraged without being lazy, and can be grateful for help without pretending that everything is fine.
He dislikes political certainty that leaves no room for evidence, correction, or the possibility that reasonable people can reach different conclusions.
skills: Experienced at inventory tracking, checking quantities, reconciling records, and spotting discrepancies between paperwork and what is physically present.
Comfortable with everyday spreadsheets, email, online banking, document storage, and video calls, though he may need help with unfamiliar account settings.
Able to compare product specifications and prices when given time, and good at noticing when an advertisement leaves out an important limitation.
Competent at planning domestic road trips, estimating drive times, identifying rest stops, and keeping a flexible backup plan.
A patient reader when material interests him; he can summarize the main point of an article and ask sensible follow-up questions.
Good at practical household troubleshooting, such as resetting a router, replacing a simple part, or following a repair video, while knowing when a licensed professional is needed.
A capable and safety-conscious driver who prefers familiar routes at night and takes breaks on longer trips.
Able to make a simple meal and follow written cooking directions, although he does not enjoy elaborate preparation or cleanup.
Can calm himself with prayer, measured breathing, a quiet walk, or writing a few thoughts down when he remembers to use those strategies before reaching his limit.
Socially perceptive in familiar settings; he notices when someone is uncomfortable, although he does not always know what to say in the moment.

relationships.name: Denise Booker
relationships.description: Terrence's older sister, with whom he shares a home. She is retired from a hospital administration career and has a steady pension. They are close enough to rely on each other but have ordinary household friction over noise, shared spaces, food, and how much advice is welcome. Denise is more structured than Terrence and will remind him about appointments; he appreciates the help more when she asks rather than tells.

relationships.name: Marcus Reed
relationships.description: Terrence's adult nephew, who also lives in the household and works remotely in a well-paid technical role. Marcus is a major contributor to the household's gross income. He is quick with devices and helps Terrence troubleshoot accounts or set up new electronics, but can move through explanations too fast. Terrence likes his company and is proud of him, while occasionally feeling that Marcus treats a question as a problem to fix instead of a conversation.

relationships.name: Elaine Booker
relationships.description: A cousin in St. Louis who keeps family stories and photographs and phones Terrence every few weeks. They share memories of older relatives and trade news about the wider family. Terrence trusts Elaine, though he sometimes lets her calls go to voicemail when his mood is low and calls back later.

relationships.name: Leonard Hayes
relationships.description: A longtime friend from Terrence's former workplace. They exchange occasional phone calls, discuss sports, retirement, and local changes, and have taken a few short fishing trips. Their friendship is comfortable with long pauses and does not require daily contact.

relationships.name: Reverend Wallace
relationships.description: The pastor of a small Baptist church Terrence attended more regularly when younger. Terrence is not a dependable weekly attendee, but he respects the pastor and occasionally speaks with him after a service or calls when he wants a calm, faith-informed perspective.

relationships.name: Former coworkers
relationships.description: He keeps light contact with several former colleagues through messages and occasional lunches. He misses the sense of being useful and known at work more than he misses the daily pressure, and he is careful not to make every conversation about his retirement.

relationships.name: Marital and parental relationships
relationships.description: Terrence has never married and has no children. He has had relationships over the years, including one serious relationship that ended before either person was ready to make a permanent commitment. He does not frame being unmarried as either a failure or a grand act of independence; it is simply how his life unfolded.

occupation.title: Student; not currently employed
occupation.organization: Public high school in Sacramento, California
occupation.description: Malik is a dependent 14-year-old student and is not expected to participate in the labor force. His main responsibilities are attending school, completing age-appropriate assignments, looking after his belongings, and doing a few ordinary household chores. He has no job, employer, professional role, or independent income. His family may give him a modest allowance, but his parents or guardians make the decisions about major purchases, transportation, and household expenses.

interests: He enjoys basketball at school and at a nearby outdoor court, especially informal games where people call their own fouls and teams change as friends arrive.
He follows professional basketball highlights more consistently than full games and likes clips that show a clever pass or a player recovering after a mistake.
He plays console video games with friends, preferring team-based games and sports games over games that require hours of solitary grinding.
He watches game tutorials when he is stuck, but dislikes videos that spend several minutes asking viewers to subscribe before getting to the explanation.
He likes making short edits of sports clips or family moments on a phone, though he usually keeps them private or sends them to a small group chat.
He enjoys music with a strong beat for walking or doing chores and sometimes asks a friend to send him a song rather than searching through a whole album.
He likes comedy and action films, especially ones he can watch with his sister without having to explain a complicated plot.
He will watch a documentary or science video if it opens with a striking question, experiment, or real-world example.
He is interested in sneakers and sports clothing, mainly noticing comfort, color, and whether an item seems too common at school.
He likes drawing logos, jersey ideas, and little diagrams in the margins of notebooks more than doing formal art exercises.
He enjoys cooking simple food with an adult because he likes being trusted with a real task and seeing the result immediately.
He likes going to parks and outdoor courts, but is less interested in a long hike described as exercise for its own sake.
He enjoys friendly board and card games when the group is small enough that everyone can follow what is happening.
He is curious about how video games are made, including character design, sound effects, and why some game controls feel better than others.
He likes browsing a bookstore or library when he is allowed to choose for himself, though he does not always finish the book he checks out.
He enjoys family gatherings when there is a cousin or another kid close to his age and an activity beyond sitting at a table with adults.
He likes visiting a new part of Sacramento with a clear destination, such as a food place, store, park, or game.
He sometimes watches creators who explain basketball tactics or review games, but quickly loses interest in content that feels staged or mean-spirited.
He enjoys learning a short dance or basketball move from a friend more than following a formal online lesson from beginning to end.
He likes small, practical challenges—beating his previous shooting score, improving an edit, or learning one new recipe—more than vague self-improvement plans.
likes: He likes chicken tacos with a flavorful salsa, but prefers to add heat gradually rather than prove he can tolerate the hottest option.
He likes rice, grilled chicken, baked potatoes, and meals where he can assemble his own plate.
He enjoys his grandmother’s macaroni and cheese and notices when someone changes the recipe, even if he will still eat it.
He likes fruit that is easy to grab, especially grapes, oranges, and cold watermelon in hot weather.
He enjoys cookies and chips as treats and does not want every snack conversation turned into a lecture about nutrition.
He likes trying a new sauce or snack if a trusted friend or relative recommends it and there is a familiar option available too.
He likes clothes that are soft, durable, and easy to move in, even if a more fashionable item looks better in a photo.
He appreciates having a few dollars of his own for a snack or small game purchase, while generally understanding that larger purchases require permission.
He likes stores where he can compare items without a salesperson following him around.
He enjoys family road trips when he can choose a playlist, take a window seat, and know how long the drive will be.
He likes receiving useful gifts that also reflect what he personally enjoys, such as a basketball, game, or team shirt.
He likes teachers who give clear instructions and do not embarrass students for asking a question.
He likes being asked for his opinion on a family plan, even when adults still make the final decision.
He likes having a quiet corner at home where he can do homework or use his phone without being in the middle of the living room.
He likes new technology when it is easy to try and does not require him to create a public profile immediately.
He likes local parks and courts where there are other people around but enough room to do his own thing.
He likes the feeling of improving at something through practice, especially when he can see the progress rather than just be told he is doing well.
He likes jokes that are clever or situational and dislikes humor that depends on humiliating someone who cannot answer back.
He likes a predictable plan for school mornings and a more flexible plan for weekends.
He likes family traditions when they feel welcoming rather than mandatory, such as a familiar holiday meal or a regular visit to his grandmother.
dislikes: He dislikes being called out in front of classmates for a mistake that could have been mentioned privately.
He dislikes adults assuming that a short answer means he is being disrespectful when he may simply be tired or thinking.
He dislikes long, repetitive homework instructions that could have been written as a short checklist.
He dislikes crowded stores when he is hungry or already tired from school.
He dislikes clothes that itch, pinch, or make it hard to move during sports.
He dislikes food that is unexpectedly very spicy, slimy, or mixed together when he expected separate ingredients.
He dislikes being made to try a new food while people watch for his reaction.
He dislikes ads and videos that interrupt what he is watching repeatedly.
He dislikes losing a game because someone changes the rules halfway through.
He dislikes friends sharing a private message or an unflattering photo without asking first.
He dislikes being rushed to make a decision about something he has not had a chance to understand.
He dislikes chores being assigned while he is in the middle of a game without any warning, even though he knows he still has to do them.
He dislikes when people treat the whole neighborhood as unsafe based on one story or a stereotype.
He dislikes very long car rides without a stop, a destination he is excited about, or something to listen to.
He dislikes adults turning every conversation about school, food, or phone use into a judgment about his character.

dimension_profile.general_attitude: He is more hopeful than gloomy about his own future, but his optimism is practical rather than automatic: he believes a bad day can improve, while also expecting adults to follow through on promises. He is open to hearing a different point of view when the person explains it without talking down to him.
dimension_profile.education_and_learning: He is an enrolled ninth grader with ordinary age-appropriate literacy and communication skills, not a high-school graduate. He learns best through examples, discussion, demonstrations, and manageable steps; he is less patient with dense instructions and can need support organizing longer work.
dimension_profile.culinary_tastes: His everyday tastes lean familiar and family-oriented, with a moderate interest in contemporary fast-casual foods and occasional new cuisines. He likes some spice but prefers to control the amount himself, enjoys meat and dairy, and is willing to eat vegetables more readily when they are part of a meal he already likes.
dimension_profile.shopping_habits: He shops occasionally and mostly with a parent or guardian, rather than making independent household purchases. He notices branding and style, but comfort, usefulness, price, and his family’s answer matter; he may compare a few options online before asking for an item and can be disappointed when the answer is no.
dimension_profile.health_consciousness: He has a modest, inconsistent interest in health. He understands that sleep, water, and movement matter, partly because his mother reminds him, but he also likes snacks and can stay on a screen later than he intended. He responds better to practical explanations than to shame or strict rules.
dimension_profile.attitude_towards_new_products: He is curious but not automatically impressed by new products. He is likely to try a game, snack, or piece of equipment after a trusted friend explains what is good about it, while being wary of expensive items that appear popular only because of advertising.
dimension_profile.cultural_influences: His daily life is locally rooted in Sacramento—school, family, friends, parks, and shops—while music, sports, games, and videos expose him to people and styles from across the country and around the world. He enjoys that mix without feeling he must adopt every trend he sees online.
dimension_profile.travel_habits: He travels occasionally with family, mostly on domestic trips by car, and enjoys going somewhere new when the plan includes familiar comforts and enough breaks. He has not traveled internationally and is curious about it, though airports and unfamiliar routines would feel easier with family beside him.
dimension_profile.cultural_background: Malik identifies as Black and African American. He has multigenerational U.S. roots: his maternal grandmother’s family has connections to Louisiana, while his father’s family has lived in California for generations. Family stories and gatherings matter to him, but he does not treat any one custom as a complete definition of who he is.
dimension_profile.lifestyle: He lives an urban family life with a mixture of school, time at home, nearby shops, parks, and car trips. He is moderately active through basketball and walking around school, but also spends substantial leisure time seated with a game or phone. His family is financially comfortable by local standards while still budgeting around housing, transportation, and other costs.

traits: He is curious when something connects to his own interests and can ask a surprisingly precise follow-up question.
He is sociable with people he knows, but usually observes the mood of a new group before joining in.
He enjoys making friends laugh and sometimes makes a joke to escape an awkward or vulnerable moment.
He is competitive during games and sports, though a loss usually bothers him more in the moment than it does the next day.
He is affectionate with close family in indirect ways, such as sharing a snack or sending a funny clip instead of saying something sentimental.
He notices unfairness quickly, especially when a rule seems to be applied differently to different students.
He can be stubborn when he thinks an adult has misunderstood him, and may argue about the wording of a request rather than do it immediately.
He is more responsible when a task has a clear deadline and visible steps than when an adult says only to “get organized.”
He likes having some say in his clothes, hobbies, and schedule, but still seeks reassurance from his mother when a decision feels consequential.
He is imaginative about possible futures but changes his mind readily as he discovers new interests.
He is sensitive to public correction and would rather receive criticism privately.
He can be impatient with repetitive explanations, even when the explanation would help him avoid a mistake.
He is capable of apologizing after he has cooled down, though he may initially defend himself or say that the other person started it.
He has a hopeful streak, but rising costs, difficult homework, or a bad game can make him briefly pessimistic.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. He likes trying unfamiliar games, music, foods, and creative projects when there is a low-pressure way to test them, but is not drawn to every new trend or abstract discussion.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate and uneven. He can be dependable about sports equipment, promises to friends, and tasks with immediate consequences; planning ahead, keeping papers in order, and starting long assignments early remain works in progress.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate. He gets energy from joking and doing activities with friends, but needs quieter time after a crowded school day and is not eager to be the center of attention among strangers.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high with people he trusts. He is helpful and considerate, though competitive, teasing, and defensive when he feels unfairly blamed.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. He has ordinary adolescent worries about fitting in, school performance, and how adults see him; he can become flustered by criticism but usually settles with time, sleep, or a conversation with someone he trusts.

beliefs: He believes that being good at something usually comes from practicing it, even if some people seem naturally better at the beginning.
He believes losing a game is frustrating but does not prove someone is bad at basketball or that they should quit.
He thinks school matters because it gives him choices later, though he does not believe every assignment is equally useful.
He believes adults should explain the reason for a rule when they can, rather than expecting a teenager to accept “because I said so” every time.
He thinks rules are fairer when they are consistent and when people are allowed to explain what happened.
He believes an apology should be about what someone did and how it affected another person, not only about ending an argument.
He thinks being funny is a good quality as long as the joke does not make someone feel trapped or humiliated.
He believes friends should not share private messages or pictures just because they can.
He thinks it is possible to disagree with a friend and still like them, although he finds that harder when the disagreement becomes personal.
He believes people should get a chance to show what they are like as individuals instead of being judged by a neighborhood, race, clothing, or one mistake.
He knows that adults worry about money and that a comfortable household still has bills; he does not assume that every request can be bought immediately.
He believes saving some of his allowance makes it easier to buy something he really wants, even though spending it on a small treat can feel better right away.
He thinks advertisements often make ordinary things look more important than they are, and that a popular product can still be disappointing.
He believes a recommendation from someone he trusts is more useful than a stranger’s dramatic online review.
He thinks new foods are worth trying when there is no pressure and he is allowed to keep a familiar option on his plate.
He believes eating well should not mean never having dessert or snacks; he understands that balance matters but does not think food should become a source of shame.
He thinks moving around helps his mood, especially when he has been sitting through classes or gaming for a long time.
He knows sleep affects how patient and focused he feels, even though he sometimes stays up later than he planned.
He believes asking for help with a school assignment is sensible, though he can feel awkward about being seen as someone who needs it.
He thinks phones can help people stay connected and learn things, but they can also make it easy to lose track of time.
He believes online popularity is not a reliable measure of whether someone is kind, talented, or worth listening to.
He thinks people should be able to enjoy music, clothes, hobbies, and games without being mocked for choosing something different.
He believes family traditions are meaningful when people explain their history and make room for younger family members to participate in their own way.
He thinks visiting a new place is exciting, but having a plan, a trusted adult, and a chance to rest makes the trip more enjoyable.
He believes that being careful around traffic, strangers, and unfamiliar places is sensible, but being afraid of every new experience would make life small.
He understands that a person can be proud of their family background while also having interests and ideas that are personal to them.
He thinks people should be able to talk about race and unfair treatment honestly, without assuming every conversation has one simple answer.
He has heard adults discuss politics and the cost of living, but he does not claim to have a settled political identity or an adult’s understanding of policy.
He thinks healthcare is important because people cannot always fix an illness or injury by themselves, though he mostly understands the issue through family conversations and school lessons.
He worries about violence when it is described in the news or near places he knows, and believes safety should be taken seriously without treating every person as dangerous.
He believes taking care of a shared park, school, or court is partly everyone’s responsibility, because people deserve places that are usable and welcoming.
skills: He can handle the basic school tasks expected of a ninth grader, including reading age-appropriate material, writing short explanations, and using a school learning platform.
He is comfortable with a smartphone, messaging, video, and common apps, but still needs adult help with privacy settings, account security, and unfamiliar online forms.
He can learn basketball drills by watching a demonstration and repeating the movement, and he has a decent sense of spacing during a casual game.
He is developing a good eye for timing and selection when editing short clips on a phone.
He can prepare a few simple foods, such as a sandwich, cereal, scrambled eggs with adult permission, or a microwave meal, and knows to ask before using unfamiliar kitchen equipment.
He remembers routes and landmarks around familiar parts of Sacramento but relies on adults for transportation and planning unfamiliar trips.
He is good at noticing when a friend is being left out, though he does not always know how to intervene without making the situation more awkward.
He can explain his preferences clearly when he feels listened to, but may become vague or defensive if he thinks an adult has already decided what he means.
He can keep track of sports gear and game accessories he cares about; he is less consistent with loose worksheets, chargers, and papers.
He knows basic safety habits, including checking for traffic, not sharing passwords, and asking a trusted adult before meeting someone he knows only online.

relationships.name: Tanya Jefferson
relationships.description: Tanya works as a registered nurse. She is warm but direct, expects Malik to attend school and contribute to ordinary chores, and asks follow-up questions when he gives a vague answer. Her work knowledge makes her attentive to health, but she tries not to turn every conversation into medical advice. Malik sometimes feels she checks his school portal too often, yet he trusts her when he is genuinely worried.

relationships.name: Darius Cole
relationships.description: Darius supervises maintenance crews for a regional public-transit agency. He is patient with practical tasks and often shows Malik how to fix or assemble something rather than doing it for him. Their relationship is friendly and steadily growing, though Malik does not always bring him personal or school concerns first.

relationships.name: Imani Jefferson
relationships.description: Imani likes spending time with Malik when she can choose the activity, especially a game, drawing, or a shared snack. He teases her about little things and can get annoyed when she enters his room without asking, but he also helps her with simple problems and does not like seeing other people pick on her.

relationships.name: Andre Jefferson
relationships.description: Andre lives in the Sacramento area and stays in contact with Malik through visits, calls, and occasional shared outings. Their plans are not perfectly regular because of work schedules, which sometimes disappoints Malik. They connect most easily around sports, music, and talking while driving.

relationships.name: Evelyn Brooks
relationships.description: Evelyn is an important family presence and shares stories about relatives and the family’s connection to Louisiana. Malik likes her cooking and enjoys hearing family history when the conversation is casual. She is affectionate, sometimes old-fashioned in her expectations, and usually willing to let him take leftovers home.

relationships.name: Jordan
relationships.description: Jordan and Malik share basketball clips, play games, and joke around between classes. They can disagree over rules or who played better, but the disagreement usually passes quickly. Malik is more open with Jordan than with most classmates, though he does not share every family concern.

relationships.name: Coach Ramirez
relationships.description: Coach Ramirez encourages effort and teamwork and corrects players without making a show of embarrassing them. Malik respects that the coach explains what needs to change instead of only calling out a mistake. He sometimes gets annoyed by conditioning drills but understands that practice is not only about playing.

relationships.name: Ms. Patel
relationships.description: Ms. Patel is approachable and gives clear assignment instructions. Malik appreciates that she allows students to ask questions without acting as if they should already know everything. He has gone to her for clarification, though he is unlikely to volunteer a long personal story in class.

occupation.title: Self-employed bookkeeper and small-business accounting services provider
occupation.organization: Whitaker Bookkeeping Services, a one-person business based in metropolitan Atlanta.
occupation.description: Douglas provides recurring bookkeeping support to a small group of local businesses, including a plumbing contractor, a neighborhood restaurant, and a two-person home-repair firm. He reconciles bank and credit-card accounts, organizes receipts, prepares payroll information, follows up on missing invoices, and produces plain-language monthly summaries. He is not a certified public accountant and does not present himself as one; he refers complex tax or audit questions to licensed professionals. He is experienced and conscientious, but he now limits the number of clients he accepts. Workload varies around payroll dates, month-end, and clients' poor record-keeping. His household income is in the $100,000–$199,999 range, but a quiet month, an unexpected expense, or a client leaving can make him anxious about the following year. He uses established accounting software and a desktop computer for essential work, but resists changing systems merely because a vendor has released a newer version.

interests: Travel, especially imagining routes and reading about places he has not yet visited.
Walking through Atlanta neighborhoods and noticing how a street changes from block to block.
Hiking on easy or moderate trails when his knee feels good.
Local history, including old street plans, preserved buildings, and the stories behind familiar districts.
Travel books, atlases, road maps, and practical guidebooks.
Small museums and historical houses that can be explored without rushing.
Public parks, tree-lined streets, and paths near water.
Listening to interviews and public radio while doing routine chores.
Reading nonfiction about history, cities, and everyday economic life.
A small amount of fiction, particularly novels with convincing characters rather than elaborate fantasy worlds.
The practical side of accounting and the satisfaction of finding where a number went wrong.
Watching a baseball game when he can follow it without having to make a whole evening of it.
Trying food from different communities in Atlanta, usually at a casual restaurant or neighborhood festival.
Observing how people use public spaces, markets, libraries, and transit.
Church music and familiar hymns, even when he is not feeling especially religious.
Gardening in pots on his balcony, mostly herbs and a few hardy plants.
Repairing small household items before deciding they need replacing.
Photography with an older, simple digital camera rather than a phone-camera upgrade.
Quiet meals with his sister or a friend.
Planning possible short trips that he may or may not actually take.
likes: A calm morning walk before the sidewalks become crowded.
A shady route with benches where he can pause without feeling conspicuous.
Crisp winter days in Atlanta and the first comfortable evenings of autumn.
A well-kept older building that has been adapted rather than demolished.
Restaurants with a short, legible menu and food that tastes prepared rather than assembled.
Vegetable dishes with beans, greens, grains, or roasted roots.
Fresh peaches, apples, citrus, and whatever fruit is in season.
A good cup of ordinary brewed coffee at home.
Unsweetened iced tea, especially in hot weather.
A quiet conversation that does not require him to defend every opinion.
People who are direct about a problem without humiliating anyone.
Printed maps and clear written directions.
Reliable tools that can be repaired or replaced without learning an app.
A clean desk with current client files in order.
Local libraries and their comfortable, unhurried atmosphere.
A modest hotel with easy parking, a quiet room, and a good shower.
A short drive to a park or historic site when a longer trip feels unrealistic.
Meditation or prayer that is practical and undramatic.
A good long walk that leaves him pleasantly tired rather than depleted.
Sharing a meal with his sister without having to organize a large family event.
dislikes: Aggressive salespeople who treat hesitation as a challenge to overcome.
New products advertised as essential before anyone explains their cost or limitations.
Phone applications that require accounts, permissions, and repeated updates for a simple task.
Crowded events where he must shout to be heard.
Being told to cheer up or make a major life change as though motivation were a switch.
Long political arguments that turn acquaintances into caricatures.
Online forms that time out or make it difficult to speak to a person.
Wasteful packaging and disposable household goods that break quickly.
Food that is excessively sweet or heavily processed.
A restaurant so noisy that conversation becomes work.
Unclear invoices and clients who expect him to reconstruct months of neglected records overnight.
Last-minute schedule changes that affect his clients or his dog.
People who confuse a confident tone with genuine expertise.
Very hot, humid afternoons when walking becomes uncomfortable.
Steep trails or uneven ground when his knee is stiff.
Being pressured to travel farther or faster than his energy permits.
Financial decisions made under urgency or fear.
Being treated as incapable simply because he is 69.
Condescending explanations of technology he has deliberately chosen not to adopt.
Arguments in which nobody seems willing to listen to the answer.
culinary_preferences: His everyday diet is mostly plant-forward, built around vegetables, beans, grains, fruit, and occasional eggs or dairy.
He is not strictly vegetarian, but meat is not the center of most meals.
He eats fish or chicken now and then, often when dining with someone else.
He likes black beans, lentils, chickpeas, and split-pea soup because they are filling and easy to keep on hand.
He enjoys collard greens, okra, tomatoes, squash, and roasted sweet potatoes.
He likes oatmeal with fruit when he has time to eat breakfast.
He buys brown rice, oats, whole-grain bread, canned beans, frozen vegetables, and fruit as practical staples.
He prefers mild-to-moderate seasoning and appreciates flavor from herbs, garlic, citrus, and vinegar.
He will try a genuinely unfamiliar cuisine if the setting feels relaxed and the menu is understandable.
He enjoys Indian, Ethiopian, Vietnamese, Mexican, and Caribbean food in Atlanta, without claiming expertise in any of them.
He likes a spicy dish when the heat does not overwhelm every other flavor.
He keeps hot sauce in the refrigerator but uses it sparingly.
He buys organic produce when the price difference is modest, especially for items he eats often.
He does not treat organic certification as a guarantee that a food is automatically healthy.
He sometimes relies on microwave grain packets, canned soup, prepared salad, or frozen meals when work runs late.
His meals can be irregular when he is absorbed in client work or too tired to cook.
He tries to keep bananas, apples, or oranges available so he has something easy to eat.
He prefers water or unsweetened tea with meals and seldom orders sugary drinks.
He enjoys a cookie or slice of pie at a church gathering but does not plan his everyday diet around dessert.
He dislikes wasting food and will turn leftovers into a second meal if they still taste good.
shopping_habits: He shops occasionally and with a list rather than browsing for entertainment.
He buys groceries in person most of the time because he likes to inspect produce and choose substitutions himself.
He uses online shopping for a specific replacement item when going to multiple stores would be inconvenient.
He compares prices but does not always buy the cheapest option; durability and familiarity matter.
He is frugal by temperament, not because he has no resources.
He is reluctant to buy new household gadgets and prefers to repair a dependable older one.
He is skeptical of subscription services and recurring charges.
He keeps receipts for business purchases and files them in a familiar system.
He rarely makes a large purchase without sleeping on it.
He may put off replacing worn shoes or a small appliance longer than is sensible.
He prefers a knowledgeable local shop for repairs when the service is fairly priced.
Rising grocery, condominium, and medical costs contribute to his sense that his finances are worse than several years ago.
travel_and_cultural_preferences: Travel is a genuine interest, though he travels rarely in practice.
He has taken only a handful of overnight trips in recent years and usually chooses a domestic destination.
Atlanta neighborhood outings, museum visits, and day trips serve as his more accessible version of exploration.
He enjoys reading about international destinations even when he has no definite booking in mind.
He favors a slower itinerary with time for a meal, a walk, and an unplanned stop.
He avoids itineraries that depend on tight connections, several hotel changes, or strenuous activity.
Cost, work coverage, fatigue, and arranging care for his dog all make travel harder to organize.
He is more comfortable traveling with one companion than joining a large tour group.
He appreciates cultural exchange and likes asking people about a dish, neighborhood, or local custom when the conversation arises naturally.
He values Atlanta's mix of Southern, Black, immigrant, and international cultural influences while also retaining affection for familiar Southern traditions.

traits: Reserved: he prefers one-on-one conversation or a small group to a large gathering.
Reflective: he thinks over a decision privately and may need a day before giving a considered answer.
Emotionally tired: he has little enthusiasm for plans and often finds it difficult to imagine that a new effort will change much.
Dependable: clients can count on him to notice a discrepancy and follow through on a promised task.
Quietly warm: he is not demonstrative, but he remembers personal details and checks on people in practical ways.
Skeptical: he is wary of sales pitches, fashionable devices, and claims that a new system will make life effortless.
Culturally curious: he enjoys encountering unfamiliar cuisines, music, and perspectives, particularly in his own city.
Cautious with money: even when he can afford a purchase, he dislikes wasting money on an item that may not last.
Dryly humorous: his jokes are understated and sometimes arrive after a beat of silence.
Stubborn: once he has settled on a familiar method, it can take a real inconvenience—not a marketing claim—to persuade him to change.
Non-confrontational: he avoids political arguments and often disengages rather than trying to win them.
Self-reliant: he takes pride in managing his own affairs but can wait too long before asking for assistance.
Compassionate in practical ways: he is more likely to offer a ride, a spreadsheet, or a meal than a grand expression of sympathy.
Patient with beginners: he explains basic financial matters without making a person feel foolish, partly because he remembers needing help himself.
Pessimistic about institutions: he expects organizations to protect themselves first, though he is not convinced that every individual within them is dishonest.

big_five.openness: Moderate overall, with an important split: he is receptive to cultural variety, conversation, art, and food, but strongly conservative about adopting new products, devices, and routines. He is more curious about people and places than about technological novelty.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderately high. He keeps client records, pays bills, and honors commitments carefully, but fatigue and low motivation sometimes delay personal errands or paperwork.
big_five.extraversion: Low. He is comfortable with clients and familiar people but recharges alone, avoids crowded social events, and does not seek to be the center of attention.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high. He is considerate and generally cooperative, though he can be terse when someone wastes his time or pressures him to buy something.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate to moderately high. Financial uncertainty, poor sleep, and an unsettled political climate can stay on his mind, but he usually contains his worry and does not share it freely.

beliefs: Markets can produce useful goods and services, but they do not reliably protect people who have little bargaining power.
Government should regulate markets where fraud, unsafe practices, or concentrated power leave ordinary people exposed.
Strong social protections can reduce poverty and insecurity without removing a person's dignity or ability to work.
Government should help provide healthcare; access to necessary treatment should not depend entirely on a person's job or ability to pay.
He supports the basic purpose of Medicare and is attentive to the costs that remain outside his coverage.
He believes abortion should be legal in most cases, while recognizing that people bring serious moral and personal convictions to the issue.
He experiences inflation as a moderate hardship: he can cover his bills, but ordinary costs have narrowed his sense of freedom.
He regards the economy as not so good, particularly because broad economic statistics do not always match what people pay each month.
His household financial situation feels worse than it did four years ago, even though his current income remains within a moderate-to-comfortable range.
He is not very confident that elections are fair in every respect, but he does not claim to know that a specific election was fraudulent.
He follows politics inconsistently and dislikes being expected to have an instant opinion on every public controversy.
He may abstain from a vote, leave a choice until late, or vote only in contests where he feels adequately informed.
He is wary of both major parties and does not feel that either represents all of his economic concerns.
Political disengagement for him is partly exhaustion; it is not proof that he has no values.
He thinks public officials should be held accountable, but he has little faith that outrage alone changes how institutions work.
He believes people should be able to disagree without treating their neighbors as enemies.
He values a safety net for older adults, disabled people, children, and workers facing a sudden loss of income.
He believes work should generally provide a measure of security, though he knows many people work hard without receiving it.
He thinks a person's financial difficulties usually have more than one cause and dislikes simplistic lectures about personal responsibility.
He supports practical measures that improve access to healthcare, food, housing, and education.
He does not assume that every expensive product is better or that every new technology represents progress.
He believes a new device should solve a real problem before it is worth learning and paying for.
He thinks digital services should retain a workable phone or in-person option for people who cannot or do not want to use an app.
He believes local shops and service businesses matter, but he understands that customers also have to manage their own budgets.
He sees cultural exchange as a normal part of living in a large city and usually welcomes it.
He believes curiosity about another culture does not require pretending that every practice is beyond criticism.
He values the kindness and music of his Christian tradition, though his faith is quieter and less certain than it was when he was younger.
Prayer and meditation can steady him even when they do not make a difficult situation disappear.
He believes religious communities are at their best when they offer concrete help and do not make people perform respectability first.
He sees walking and ordinary exercise as worthwhile forms of care, not as a substitute for medical treatment.
He believes a healthful diet should be affordable and convenient enough to fit into real working lives.
He thinks organic food can be a reasonable preference when affordable, but it should not become a status test.
He believes travel can broaden a person's understanding, but nobody is morally deficient for being unable to afford it.
He values privacy and thinks companies should collect less personal data than they commonly do.
He believes one can be concerned about democracy without spending every day consuming political news.
He is uneasy about public distrust and political violence, but has little appetite for speculative arguments about what might happen.
He thinks experience has made him more cautious, not necessarily wiser about every subject.
He regards dependable relationships and small acts of help as more meaningful than public displays of virtue.
skills: Accurately reconciles business bank statements, card transactions, invoices, and receipts.
Recognizes common bookkeeping errors, duplicate payments, and missing documentation.
Prepares organized monthly financial summaries for owners who are not trained in accounting.
Handles payroll records and routine bookkeeping schedules for small businesses.
Explains financial information in plain language without assuming the client knows accounting terminology.
Maintains long-term professional relationships with clients and remembers their recurring needs.
Uses desktop accounting software, spreadsheets, email, and online banking for essential work.
Can learn a stable software process but is slower and more reluctant when an interface is frequently redesigned.
Plans walking routes and can read a printed road map or street map comfortably.
Can cook several uncomplicated, nourishing meals from pantry staples.
Has a practical eye for whether a household item can be repaired or should be replaced.
Listens patiently and often notices when someone is worried about money but embarrassed to say so.

relationships.name: Ellen Whitaker
relationships.description: Ellen lives in the Atlanta metropolitan area with her husband. They speak most weeks and see one another for a meal every month or two. She is more socially active and sometimes urges Douglas to travel or join a group; he appreciates the concern but dislikes being managed. He helps her with occasional financial paperwork, while she is more likely to notice when he sounds unusually tired.

relationships.name: Chris
relationships.description: Ellen's adult son works in a technical field and is patient when helping Douglas with a necessary computer or phone issue. Douglas likes him but can become prickly if the help starts with an assumption that all of Douglas's habits need upgrading.

relationships.name: Leon
relationships.description: Leon is a former colleague from Douglas's earlier accounting work. They meet for coffee or an inexpensive lunch several times a year and exchange short phone calls. Their friendship is comfortable enough to tolerate long pauses and occasional disagreements about politics.

relationships.name: Patch
relationships.description: Patch is a medium-sized mixed-breed dog who gives Douglas a reason to get outside at set times. Caring for him constrains spontaneous overnight travel, but Douglas does not resent the responsibility.

relationships.name: Miriam
relationships.description: Miriam sometimes invites him to a meal or a cultural event. She is more openly enthusiastic than he is, and he accepts invitations when they are modest and do not require a full day of socializing.

relationships.name: Small-business clients
relationships.description: A handful of owners rely on Douglas for steady bookkeeping. Their trust matters to him, although he sometimes feels worn down by clients who submit records late and then expect him to make a deadline effortless.

relationships.name: Household
relationships.description: Douglas has never married and has no spouse, partner, or child living with him. His home is his own responsibility, with family and friends available for occasional support rather than daily care.

Lucía Reyes.nationality: American; a U.S. resident and citizen born in Houston, Texas.

occupation.title: Infant; not employed
occupation.organization: Not applicable
occupation.description: Lucía is not in the labor force and has no job, professional role, income, or workplace. She is a wholly dependent infant. Her day consists of sleep, feeding, diaper changes, closeness with caregivers, and short periods of alert sensory exploration. She cannot shop, make decisions about products, or take responsibility for household tasks.

preferences.developmental_caveat: These are caregiver-observed sensory responses and emerging patterns, not considered choices or fully formed tastes. They can change quickly and are affected by hunger, fatigue, temperature, and health.
observable_likes_and_engagement: Often attends to the familiar sound of her mother’s voice when it is close and calm.
Frequently looks toward her father when he speaks from beside her.
Appears interested in faces at close range, especially during a quiet moment after waking.
Sometimes responds to a familiar voice with coos or a brief smile.
Often relaxes when held securely against a caregiver’s chest.
Usually prefers gentle, steady rocking over sudden bouncing or abrupt changes in position.
Can enjoy being carried upright after a feeding while an adult supports her head and body.
Sometimes watches a slowly moving, high-contrast toy during supervised awake time.
Responds to soft singing, especially when a caregiver repeats the same short song.
May become absorbed by a familiar lullaby even when she does not fall asleep immediately.
Often enjoys short periods of looking at a sturdy board book with clear pictures while held.
Shows interest in a caregiver’s face during simple peekaboo-like exchanges, though the game is brief.
May enjoy the sensation of a clean, soft cotton cloth against her hands during supervised play.
Frequently brings her hands toward her mouth and seems interested in exploring them.
Can enjoy gentle, supervised tummy time in short stretches when rested.
Sometimes watches sunlight or shadows on a wall, provided the light is not harsh or directed into her eyes.
Often settles after a warm, unhurried bath when she is not already overtired.
May become calm during a slow walk in her stroller with a familiar adult nearby.
Usually takes comfort from a clean diaper, comfortable clothing, and being returned to a familiar routine.
Appears more receptive to play after a nap and feeding than when approaching her usual rest time.
observable_discomfort_or_overload: Communicates hunger or the need for comfort by fussing or crying; she cannot explain which need is present.
May cry more sharply when a feeding is delayed beyond her cues.
Often becomes unsettled when she is overtired, even if the room is otherwise calm.
May turn her face away or fuss when several people speak to her at once.
Can startle at sudden loud sounds such as a dropped object or a slammed door.
May resist a hurried change of position, particularly when already tired.
Can become fussy in a wet or soiled diaper and usually settles after an adult changes her.
May dislike being too warm in Houston’s humid weather; caregivers check her clothing and comfort rather than assuming she is cold.
Sometimes fusses during a car ride before she settles, especially if the trip overlaps with sleep or feeding.
May cry during a clothing change if she is cold, hungry, or impatient, rather than because she has a settled dislike of dressing.
Can lose interest in a toy or face after a short period and need a quieter pause.
May protest when put down after being held, though this varies and is not a deliberate demand for attention.
Sometimes pulls away from a bottle when she needs a pause or has had enough, and caregivers follow her feeding cues.
May fuss in a crowded, noisy waiting room and settle better in a quieter place.
Does not yet reliably distinguish discomfort from tiredness in a way adults can interpret without context.
food_and_culinary_experience: Her nourishment is caregiver-provided breast milk and infant formula; she has no independent food choices.
Her family uses a combination-feeding routine that fits the mother’s return to work and the childcare schedule.
She has not begun solids. Her parents plan to discuss readiness and timing with her pediatrician rather than infer a culinary preference from interest in watching adults eat.
Spicy, traditional, modern, vegetarian, and meat-based cuisines are not meaningful personal preferences for her at this age.
She has no known food allergy so far, but her limited exposure means that absence of a known allergy is not a guarantee about future foods.

age_appropriate_dimensions.general_attitude: Lucía has no articulated outlook, optimism, pessimism, or open-mindedness; caregivers observe whether she is settled, curious-looking, tired, or distressed in the moment.
age_appropriate_dimensions.education: Formal education is not applicable; her current learning consists of ordinary infant sensory and social development.
age_appropriate_dimensions.culinary_tastes: Not yet established. Adults decide what milk she receives, and she has not developed a broad palate or chosen between traditional and modern food.
age_appropriate_dimensions.shopping_habits: She does not shop or make purchasing decisions. Her parents buy diapers, formula, clothing, and equipment according to safety, availability, and household budget.
age_appropriate_dimensions.health_consciousness: She cannot make health decisions. Her caregivers arrange pediatric visits, follow safe-sleep guidance, and seek medical advice when something worries them.
age_appropriate_dimensions.attitude_toward_new_products: She is not a product evaluator. Her response to a new toy or bottle is an immediate sensory reaction, while adults decide whether an item is safe and useful.
age_appropriate_dimensions.cultural_influences: She is being raised amid Houston’s local and globally varied urban environment, with family exposure to Mexican-American and Salvadoran-American customs and both English and Spanish.
age_appropriate_dimensions.travel_habits: She travels only with adults, mainly on short car trips around Houston and occasional family visits within Texas; she has no independent travel preferences.
age_appropriate_dimensions.cultural_background: Her family background is Latino and U.S.-based, with Mexican-American and Salvadoran-American roots. Her own sense of identity will develop over time rather than being presumed from ancestry.
age_appropriate_dimensions.lifestyle: Her life is necessarily dependent and mostly home- and caregiver-centered. Houston’s urban setting means car travel is common, while her play and movement are limited to age-appropriate, supervised activity.

personality.developmental_caveat: At four months, stable adult personality traits cannot be confidently assigned. The descriptions below are provisional observations of temperament and current behavior, not fixed character judgments.
traits: Often becomes visibly attentive when a familiar caregiver speaks close by.
Can be socially responsive, especially during calm face-to-face interaction, but does not engage on demand every time.
Sometimes smiles during familiar routines; the smile is an observable response, not proof of a particular thought.
Has variable tolerance for stimulation and may look away, fuss, or stiffen when a room becomes busy.
Usually settles more readily with a known caregiver’s voice, warmth, or gentle rocking than with an unfamiliar handling style.
Can become quite vocal when comfortable, producing coos and short squeals rather than purposeful speech.
Shows ordinary infant frustration when hungry, tired, wet, or unable to settle, with crying that can intensify if the need is not addressed.
Is still learning to coordinate her attention and body; she may reach toward something and miss it, then try again later.
May be watchful in a new setting before relaxing, although her response varies with sleep, hunger, and who is holding her.
Has short windows of alert play and needs adult help to shift back to rest before she becomes overtired.
Can enjoy repeated songs or simple games but does not insist on a particular activity or understand its rules.
Relies on adults to notice her cues; she is not deliberately manipulative, stubborn, or independent.

big_five.openness: Not meaningfully measurable as a stable personality trait at four months. In the narrow sense of observed novelty response, she sometimes watches a new sound or object briefly and sometimes turns away; the response depends strongly on her state and the setting.
big_five.conscientiousness: Not applicable as an adult trait. She has no planning, self-discipline, or task completion; predictable caregiver routines are imposed by adults rather than organized by her.
big_five.extraversion: Not meaningfully measurable as a stable trait. She is sometimes animated during quiet interaction with familiar people and sometimes quiet or tired, with no dependable adult-like social preference yet.
big_five.agreeableness: Not applicable as a moral or interpersonal trait. She can be soothed by gentle, familiar care, but crying or resisting a position is a signal of need or discomfort, not unkindness or defiance.
big_five.neuroticism: Not validly scored at this age. Her distress is ordinary infant signaling and varies with sleep, hunger, illness, stimulation, and comfort; it should not be treated as an enduring anxiety tendency.

beliefs.status: Lucía has no articulated beliefs, political opinions, religious commitments, or settled views. The observations below describe developmental limits and simple emerging familiarity; they should not be portrayed as adult convictions.
developmental_observations: She cannot state or explain a belief about who she is.
She has no developed understanding of what it means to be American or to live in Texas.
She cannot describe a racial, ethnic, national, or cultural identity.
She has no articulated religious belief or understanding of religious practice.
She has no political affiliation and cannot understand parties, elections, or government.
She has no opinion about economic conditions, household income, or the cost of goods.
She cannot understand healthcare policy, insurance, medical institutions, or public health debates.
She has no view about immigration, citizenship, borders, or legal status.
She cannot form an opinion about climate change or environmental policy.
She has no concept of gun policy, crime, policing, or public safety as social issues.
She does not understand fairness as an abstract moral principle, though she can signal immediate discomfort.
She cannot distinguish truth from a lie or judge whether a statement is sincere.
She has no understanding of rules, duties, rights, or consequences in the adult sense.
She may become familiar with recurring caregivers, but this is not a reasoned belief about family roles.
She can respond differently to familiar and unfamiliar voices without holding an explicit belief about trust.
She may anticipate repeated care sequences, such as being held before a feed, but does not understand a schedule conceptually.
She has no developed understanding of time, dates, birthdays, or the future.
She cannot plan for adulthood or imagine a future occupation.
She has no personal ambition or long-term purpose; future hopes belong to her parents.
She has no concept of money, saving, spending, debt, or wealth.
She cannot decide whether a product is good, bad, necessary, or worth its price.
She has no established preference for organic, conventional, local, or imported goods.
She cannot form a dietary philosophy or choose between vegetarian and meat-based eating.
She has no understanding of language labels; hearing English and Spanish does not mean she can identify either language.
She cannot yet describe or choose among cultural traditions.
She has no abstract view about gender roles or personal identity.
She does not hold an opinion about education, school, or academic achievement.
She has no considered view about travel, other countries, or unfamiliar cultures.
She cannot meaningfully evaluate risk or make safety judgments; adults must provide protection.
Her observable reactions to sound, faces, touch, or routines are immediate developmental responses, not evidence of a philosophical worldview.

skills: Can briefly track a nearby face or slowly moving object with her eyes, though attention is short and inconsistent.
Recognizes familiar voices and may orient toward them when alert.
Produces coos, squeals, cries, and other early vocal sounds; these are communication precursors, not words.
Brings her hands toward her mouth and is beginning to explore her hands and nearby safe objects.
Can hold her head more steadily than a newborn but still needs appropriate support and supervision.
Shows early social responses such as looking at a caregiver’s face or smiling at times.
Signals discomfort and needs through changes in crying, expression, movement, and settling; adults must interpret those cues.
Has no independent self-care, language, reading, walking, feeding, safety, or decision-making skills.

relationships.name: Marisol Reyes
relationships.description: Marisol is an elementary-school teacher. She is one of Lucía’s primary caregivers and is familiar with her feeding cues, the way she settles when held, and the difference between a tired fuss and a more urgent cry. Returning to work has made childcare coordination and pumping or preparing feeds part of the family’s practical routine.

relationships.name: Javier Reyes
relationships.description: Javier works as an electrical project estimator. He participates in daily care, including bottle feeds, diaper changes, and settling Lucía after work. His schedule can run late during busy periods, so the family’s division of care changes from day to day.

relationships.name: Elena Reyes
relationships.description: Elena lives in the Houston area and helps with childcare when her schedule allows, usually one weekday. Lucía is familiar with her voice and being held by her, although she is too young to understand kinship labels.

relationships.name: Rosa Reyes and Miguel Reyes
relationships.description: They live elsewhere in Texas and visit when work and travel permit. Lucía has seen them a few times; adults recognize them as family, while Lucía’s response is simply to familiar or unfamiliar faces and voices.

relationships.name: Childcare caregivers
relationships.description: Lucía attends a small licensed childcare center several weekdays. Staff provide feeds, naps, diaper changes, and supervised age-appropriate play, and communicate basic daily information to her parents.

occupation.title: Hotel laundry and housekeeping associate
occupation.organization: A mid-sized downtown Memphis hotel
occupation.employment_status: Employed about 32–36 hours a week, usually on overnight or rotating shifts. She receives an hourly wage and occasional shift differential; extra hours are available but she cannot always take them because of pain, fatigue, and family responsibilities.
occupation.description: Shannon handles commercial laundry and linen work and helps with practical room-turnover tasks when the hotel is short-staffed. She sorts sheets and towels, runs washers and dryers, moves linen carts, checks that supplies are in the expected locations, and alerts a supervisor when equipment is malfunctioning or a room needs attention. She is not a manager, though newer employees sometimes ask her where things go because she knows the building and its routines.
occupation.workplace_strengths: She is observant, quick with hands-on tasks, good at recognizing a problem before it becomes a larger mess, and candid about what can realistically be completed in a shift. She can remember a route or procedure after seeing it demonstrated. She is not comfortable with paperwork or written notices and relies on a supervisor or a coworker to read unfamiliar forms aloud.
occupation.constraints_and_accommodations: Rheumatoid arthritis and persistent joint pain make repetitive lifting and long periods on her feet difficult, especially during a flare. Her supervisor allows short recovery breaks when staffing permits, and Shannon uses a cart rather than carrying heavy bundles by hand. She uses voice-to-text and text-to-speech on her phone for work messages and appointment reminders. These tools help her manage limited literacy and spare her hands some typing; she does not present herself as an expert in accessibility or technology.
occupation.work_attitude: She takes pride in being useful and dislikes being treated as unreliable because she sometimes needs a modified task or a spoken explanation. She will cover a shift for a coworker she trusts, but becomes blunt when managers make last-minute demands and assume she can absorb unlimited extra work.

interests: Cooking filling dinners for her household, especially meals that can be reheated after an overnight shift.
Baking cookies or a simple cake with her daughter when they have an overlapping day off.
Console gaming, mostly familiar games she can return to without relearning complicated menus.
Mobile puzzle and word-free matching games while riding the bus or waiting at a clinic.
Watching cooking competitions and home renovation shows, even when she thinks the contestants make avoidable mistakes.
