Following a few local news stories when they affect transit, schools, neighborhood safety, or hospital access.
Listening to family members talk about older relatives and the way Memphis neighborhoods have changed.
Browsing short videos about recipes, game tips, and household fixes.
Taking short walks through busy parts of her neighborhood when her joints are cooperating.
Visiting a nearby park or riverfront with her daughter for an inexpensive change of scenery.
Listening to music while folding laundry at home, especially familiar R&B, country, gospel, and older pop songs.
Watching comedy clips and rewatching television episodes she already knows.
Trying a new restaurant when a relative recommends it and can explain what to order.
Looking through discount-store aisles when she has a concrete errand, though she does not enjoy extended browsing.
Playing a board or card game with family during a holiday gathering, provided nobody turns it into a serious argument.
Keeping an eye out for practical apartment solutions, such as a sturdier shower mat or a better way to organize groceries.
Talking with a trusted coworker during a quiet stretch of a shift.
Planning short trips to visit relatives or see a nearby beach, city, or park.
Watching football highlights or a major game when someone in the family has it on.
Making familiar comfort food for church or extended-family gatherings.
Learning a game mechanic or recipe through demonstration rather than written instructions.
Sharing funny stories about customers, relatives, or small workplace mishaps with people she trusts.
likes: Meat-centered meals such as baked chicken, burgers, pork chops, sausage, and roast meat.
Familiar Southern sides such as macaroni and cheese, green beans, cornbread, mashed potatoes, and rice.
Food that is well-seasoned but not so spicy that it overwhelms the rest of the meal.
Cookies, especially chocolate chip or soft sugar cookies, as a late-night treat.
Sweet tea and cold soda, even though she knows she drinks more of them than is ideal.
A hot meal after work when the apartment is quiet and nobody needs anything from her.
Cooking enough food for leftovers so she does not need to buy dinner during a tiring shift.
A game with a clear goal, responsive controls, and no pressure to compete online.
Playing a familiar console game beside her daughter, with each of them commenting on the other's choices.
Phone features that read messages aloud or let her dictate a response.
People who explain an unfamiliar process without making her feel slow.
A supervisor who gives direct instructions and follows through on agreed accommodations.
Bus routes that run often enough that she does not have to plan an entire day around one connection.
Walking to a corner shop for one needed item rather than making a long trip to a large store.
Discounts on household staples and a good sale on meat that can be frozen.
Clean, dry sheets and a comfortable pillow after an overnight shift.
Comedy that is a little irreverent but not mean about someone else's disability or reading difficulty.
Family gatherings where food is abundant and people can talk without a formal agenda.
Church-homecoming meals and holiday traditions even though she rarely attends services.
A short domestic trip with a clear plan, convenient stops, and somewhere comfortable to sit.
Being told honestly when a product has a flaw before she spends money on it.
Small comforts that feel earned after a hard stretch, including a snack, a new game, or a takeout meal.
dislikes: Being handed a dense form and told to figure it out without anyone offering to explain it.
People who mistake limited reading ability for low intelligence or lack of effort.
A manager changing a shift at the last minute and acting as if family responsibilities are irrelevant.
Being pressured to buy a product before she has had time to ask someone she trusts about it.
Salespeople who use technical language to hide the cost or conditions of a deal.
Very elaborate menus that do not make it clear what a dish contains.
Vegetarian substitutes presented as if they should automatically be more appealing to her than familiar meat dishes.
Food that is bland, dry, or served cold when it should be hot.
Extreme heat when she is already tired from a shift and her joints are aching.
Standing in a long line with nowhere to sit.
Noisy public spaces where it is difficult to hear what another person is saying.
Being told to calm down before anyone has listened to what she is actually upset about.
People who promise to help her mother and then do not show up.
Coworkers who leave a mess for the next shift and insist it is not their responsibility.
Written-only communication about a schedule change or an important appointment.
Having her phone battery die when she needs transit directions or spoken text.
Spending an entire day on errands with no time to rest or eat properly.
Expensive subscription services that keep charging after a free trial.
A game that depends on complicated reading, constant online chat, or fast reactions when her hands hurt.
Being treated as if a disability means she cannot make her own decisions.
Persistent unsolicited health advice from people who do not know her circumstances.
A household budget discussion framed as blame rather than problem-solving.

traits: Skeptical by default: she wants to know who benefits from a proposal and what the catch might be.
Blunt in disagreement, especially when she feels someone is being evasive or patronizing.
Guarded with new people, but not incapable of warmth; trust usually comes from repeated behavior rather than charm.
Competitive in small, everyday ways, such as wanting to finish a task well or prove that she can keep up.
Protective of her daughter and mother, sometimes stepping in before either has asked for help.
Open-minded and curious in conversation; she can revise a view when someone gives her a credible reason, even if she dislikes admitting she changed her mind.
Practical and hands-on, preferring an example she can see over a lengthy explanation.
Proud, particularly about managing her household and staying employed despite limitations.
Funny in a dry, sometimes teasing way; humor helps her handle awkwardness and fatigue.
Impatient with bureaucracy, long waits, and instructions that assume everyone reads comfortably.
Loyal to people who have shown up for her, but capable of holding a grudge when she feels exploited.
Emotionally more sensitive than her tough presentation suggests; she can replay a dismissive remark for days.
Resourceful about making a meal, a shift, or a small amount of money stretch.
Occasionally impulsive with treats and small purchases, particularly when she feels she has had a hard week.
Not naturally meticulous about paperwork or schedules, but reliable about familiar work routines and promises that matter to family.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. She is interested in unfamiliar perspectives, new games, and different people's stories, and can reconsider an opinion. She is less drawn to novelty in products and routines unless she has a reason to trust the change.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate and uneven. She is dependable with a shift, family appointment, or task she has learned by demonstration, but struggles with paperwork, long-range planning, and maintaining savings. Her consistency is strongest when another person is counting on her.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. She can be lively and talkative among familiar coworkers or relatives, but large groups and unfamiliar social events tire her. She does not seek constant company and values having a corner of the apartment to herself.
big_five.agreeableness: Low to moderate. She is not automatically accommodating and can be argumentative, guarded, and difficult to redirect in a conflict. She is also protective, capable of generosity, and fair-minded when she believes others are being treated badly.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderately high. Financial and health uncertainty can make her irritable or worried, and criticism can linger. She is not constantly distressed; humor, familiar routines, family contact, and a sense of being useful help her recover.

beliefs: Personal liberty matters, and adults should have room to make ordinary decisions about their own lives without needless government interference.
Privacy is important; she dislikes the feeling that a company, employer, or government office can demand more personal information than it needs.
Rules should be understandable and applied consistently rather than used selectively against people with less money or influence.
She is wary of promises that a new policy will fix a complicated problem immediately.
She is open to hearing an argument that differs from hers, but trusts a concrete explanation more than a slogan.
She leans libertarian in her general politics and does not feel fully represented by either major party.
She supports unions, collective bargaining, and worker protections because an individual employee has little leverage when dealing with a large employer alone.
She thinks a union should answer to its members and should not pressure workers into silence about problems.
Workplace safety is not a luxury; people should not have to choose between a paycheck and avoiding an injury.
A person who works hard should receive predictable wages, reasonable breaks, and clear information about scheduling.
She thinks employers should make practical accommodations when a worker can still do the essential parts of a job.
She does not believe needing an accommodation means someone is lazy or asking for special treatment.

She believes abortion should be illegal in most cases because she regards unborn life as morally significant, while accepting exceptions when a pregnancy seriously threatens the pregnant person's life.
She finds the legal details around abortion difficult and does not claim to have a tidy answer for every circumstance.
She sees gun violence as a very big problem, especially when it affects children, schools, and ordinary neighborhood life.
She supports sensible steps that keep guns away from people who pose a credible danger, while remaining cautious about broad rules that disregard lawful ownership.
She believes mental-health care and practical community support should be part of any serious response to violence.
She thinks local safety depends on people trusting one another and being able to contact someone who will respond, not only on politicians making speeches.
She is Christian by culture and family tradition, and believes faith can offer comfort and a language for compassion.
She rarely attends services and is uncomfortable when people use religion to shame others or pretend every family has the same life.
She values her family's church traditions, shared meals, holiday gatherings, and the sense that people know one another.
She believes a person's character is shown more by how they treat vulnerable people than by how often they announce their beliefs.
She regards family responsibility as important, but also believes one person cannot be expected to meet every need without help.
Parents should be involved in their children's lives, even after divorce, as long as involvement is safe and respectful.
Her daughter should be encouraged to finish school, but she does not think a diploma makes someone automatically wise or a person without one automatically incapable.
She believes practical skills and spoken knowledge are real forms of intelligence, even when schools and employers reward written credentials.
She thinks adults who struggle with reading deserve patient, private support rather than public embarrassment.
She sees inflation as a serious concern in general, but says it has not caused her household direct hardship because they have still managed to cover basic needs.
She nevertheless feels her family's financial situation is worse than it was four years ago, because the household has less room for unexpected costs and less confidence about the future.
She describes the economy as not so good: people she knows are working, but basic expenses and insecure schedules make it hard to feel settled.
She believes saving money is sensible, but understands why a person living close to the edge may spend on small comforts rather than maintain a perfect emergency fund.
She thinks government should be limited in some personal and economic decisions, but that this does not excuse employers from treating workers fairly.
She believes elections are generally legitimate, though she is only somewhat confident that every part of the process is fair and well-run.
She is uneasy about political violence and thinks people should be able to disagree without threatening one another.
She believes local experience is often more useful than a national argument that ignores what a neighborhood actually needs.
She values directness, but has learned that being blunt can hurt someone who is already ashamed or afraid; she tries, with mixed success, to be clearer rather than crueler.
She thinks new products should prove dependable before she abandons something familiar, especially when money is tight.
She does not consider indulgent food a moral failure and is not currently motivated to turn every meal into a health decision.
She believes taking care of her health matters, but sees pain, shift work, transportation, time, and money as real barriers rather than simple excuses.
She thinks people can be both tough and in need of help, and dislikes the expectation that family members must hide every difficulty.
skills: Strong practical memory for familiar sequences, routes, equipment locations, and hands-on procedures.
Good at noticing unusual sounds, smells, or changes in how hotel laundry equipment is operating.
Comfortable sorting, folding, stacking, and moving linens efficiently when pain is manageable.
Can explain a practical problem clearly in conversation, particularly when she has seen it happen herself.
Capable of staying calm and speaking firmly with an upset guest once she understands what the person needs.
Good at stretching groceries and turning leftovers into another meal.
Experienced with basic home cooking and straightforward baking.
Knows the local bus system well enough to plan familiar trips and identify a workable backup route.
Uses smartphone voice typing, read-aloud functions, spoken reminders, and familiar icons to manage communication and appointments.
Can learn a new game or household task quickly when someone demonstrates it rather than relying on printed instructions.
Good at recognizing when she or a family member needs a rest, even though she sometimes ignores her own warning signs.
Able to set a clear boundary when she believes a supervisor or relative is asking too much.

relationships.name: Janice Whitlock
relationships.description: Janice lives with Shannon and contributes retirement and disability income toward household costs. She has mobility limitations and needs help with some appointments, shopping, and heavier tasks. They are close but can clash when Janice criticizes Shannon's spending or Shannon feels that the caregiving burden is being taken for granted.

relationships.name: Maya Whitlock
relationships.description: Maya lives primarily with Shannon and spends some weekends with her father. Shannon is protective and wants her to finish school and have choices, but their relationship includes ordinary arguments about chores, phone use, and independence. Maya sometimes helps with phone messages or reads a letter aloud, though Shannon tries not to make her daughter feel responsible for adult paperwork.

relationships.name: Aaron Whitlock
relationships.description: Aaron has a separate household and shares parenting responsibilities. Their communication is mostly about schedules, school, and expenses. They can be civil and cooperative when both are focused on Maya, but unresolved resentments from the divorce make money discussions tense.

relationships.name: Karen Whitlock
relationships.description: Karen lives elsewhere in the Memphis area, works a different schedule, and is one of the few people Shannon will call when she needs a ride or help understanding a complicated letter. Karen is caring but cannot take on a regular caregiving role, which Shannon sometimes resents even while knowing it is not entirely fair.

relationships.name: Rochelle
relationships.description: Rochelle has worked at the hotel longer than Shannon and knows which supervisors are dependable. She will read a work notice aloud without making a spectacle of it, and Shannon returns the favor by covering tasks when Rochelle has a difficult shift. Their friendship is frank and occasionally argumentative.

relationships.name: Denise
relationships.description: Denise knows Shannon is capable at the practical parts of the job and gives instructions verbally when possible. She is supportive about breaks but also under pressure to keep staffing costs down, so Shannon does not assume every accommodation will be honored without asking.

relationships.name: Reverend Calhoun
relationships.description: He leads the congregation her mother has known for years. Shannon sees him mainly at holiday events, homecoming meals, or family occasions. She respects his care for older members but does not want him or anyone else treating church attendance as proof of whether she is a good person.

occupation.title: Part-time food-preparation worker and prep cook
occupation.organization: A contractor-operated kitchen serving a regional hospital near Cookeville, Tennessee
occupation.description: Shane prepares vegetables, portions ingredients, assembles simple meals, restocks a service line, labels food, and helps with cleanup. He is dependable with repetitive hands-on work and has learned to keep multiple prep tasks moving without getting in the way of cooks working the hot line. He is usually scheduled for roughly 26 to 32 hours a week, but coverage needs, staffing changes, and seasonal fluctuations can alter his hours. He has little control over the schedule and may be asked to stay late or cover a shift at short notice. The job offers limited benefits, and his income is too low to make unexpected unpaid time off easy. He follows kitchen sanitation procedures carefully and is matter-of-fact about dietary accommodations, including preparing vegetarian options, although he is not responsible for designing menus. His own vegetarian diet can mean he brings food from home rather than relying on staff meals. His household income, combining his variable earnings with his wife's intermittent part-time work, is below $25,000 a year.

interests: Walking on wooded roads and maintained local trails, especially early in the morning before traffic and heat build.
Hiking at a comfortable pace with his wife, stopping to look at plants or a view rather than treating the walk as a race.
Fishing from shore or a small public-access spot when a friend can lend him basic gear.
Cycling short distances on quiet roads, though he avoids routes where traffic feels unsafe.
Camping occasionally in a simple site where they can bring their own food and avoid expensive equipment rentals.
Arts, crafts, and DIY projects, particularly small repairs and handmade gifts that use materials already around the house.
Fixing loose cabinet hinges, patching a screen, sharpening kitchen knives, and other repairs that make a home feel more manageable.
Watching practical repair videos and saving instructions even when he does not have the money or tools to try the project immediately.
Browsing phone and computer reviews, comparing models, and reading comments from people who have used a device for more than a week.
International music and film, including unfamiliar material found through streaming recommendations or shared by friends online.
Gospel and Christian music, especially recordings that sound like people singing together rather than a highly polished production.
Country, folk, old rock, and acoustic music that he can listen to while driving or doing repetitive kitchen work.
Reading accessible nonfiction, travel writing, biographies, and occasional mysteries borrowed from the library.
Watching documentaries and straightforward how-to videos, although he sometimes wanders into unrelated clips afterward.
Following a few local Facebook groups for road closures, community events, lost pets, and recommendations for reliable mechanics.
Making simple vegetarian meals from beans, rice, potatoes, lentils, vegetables, and whatever is on sale.
Trying a new recipe when the ingredients are affordable and the recipe does not require a specialty appliance.
Quiet visits with his wife or one trusted friend rather than a large group meal.
Church service projects where the task is concrete, such as preparing food or helping an older member with a small repair.
Planning a trip with maps, lodging options, travel documents, and a realistic ceiling for what they can spend.
likes: A quiet trail after light rain, when the air is cool and the ground is not yet muddy.
The clean, warm smell of bread or coffee in a kitchen before the main rush begins.
A phone with a bright screen, dependable battery, and a camera that works well in ordinary indoor light.
Used or refurbished technology that comes with a real return policy and a clear explanation of its condition.
Online reviews that describe drawbacks as well as advantages instead of sounding like advertising.
Being able to compare prices from home instead of driving to several stores across the county.
A filling bowl of lentil soup, vegetable chili, beans and rice, or potatoes with greens.
Spicy food in moderate amounts, especially hot sauce added at the table so everyone can adjust it.
Fresh fruit when it is affordable, particularly apples, bananas, oranges, and whatever is in season locally.
The satisfaction of finishing a repair with a basic tool rather than paying someone for a small job.
A church service that feels sincere, unhurried, and welcoming to people who do not have polished clothes or confident answers.
People who speak plainly about money and do not make hardship sound like a personal moral failure.
A small group of friends who can sit together without having to fill every pause.
A low-cost trip built around walking, public places, local food, and visiting someone they know.
International neighborhoods, music, and food that give him a glimpse of lives unlike his own.
Simple, comfortable clothes with pockets and fabric that can take repeated washing.
A predictable work shift posted far enough in advance to arrange transportation and home responsibilities.
Useful gifts such as a sturdy water bottle, a good flashlight, or a repair kit.
Journaling briefly when his thoughts are tangled, especially after a stressful conversation.
Prayer and quiet breathing when he is worried but cannot immediately change the situation.
dislikes: Being pressured to buy an expensive product because a salesperson says the offer expires today.
Online checkout pages that hide shipping costs, fees, or financing terms until the last step.
Devices that require a subscription for basic functions he expected to own outright.
People who make jokes about low-wage workers while depending on their labor.
Being told to solve a financial problem by simply budgeting harder when the essentials already exceed what comes in.
A work schedule changed at the last moment without acknowledgment that other people rely on his time.
Crowded stores with loud announcements and narrow aisles, particularly after a long shift.
Being treated as ignorant because he did not attend college.
Food waste, particularly when edible food is discarded while people are struggling to afford groceries.
Meat-heavy meals being presented as the only substantial option at a family or church gathering.
Overly sweet drinks and desserts that leave a sticky aftertaste.
Expensive wellness advice that assumes a person has flexible hours, plenty of money, and easy access to appointments.
Political arguments that require him to defend a whole party instead of discussing a particular policy.
Corporate language that promises a family-like workplace while hours and benefits remain insecure.
Long paperwork forms with confusing instructions and no person available to answer a basic question.
Social media arguments that turn every disagreement into a public contest.
Being expected to talk about private family problems before he has decided he trusts someone.
Trails or campsites with loud music playing late at night.
Unreliable car repairs and mechanics who cannot provide a clear estimate.
Feeling that a purchase has created another monthly obligation he cannot easily cancel.
culinary_preferences: He follows a vegetarian diet and usually avoids meat and fish; he does not insist that other people eat the same way.
His vegetarianism is partly ethical and environmental, but it is also a practical habit that has become familiar over time.
He will ask whether broth, lard, or meat drippings are used in a dish rather than assuming a vegetable-looking meal is vegetarian.
He prefers familiar Southern staples adapted without meat, including beans, greens, cornbread made without animal fat, and vegetable casseroles.
He likes beans and rice because the ingredients are filling, inexpensive, and easy to prepare in batches.
Lentils are a favored protein when they are on sale, although he does not enjoy every lentil texture.
He likes roasted potatoes, sweet potatoes, and onions, especially when browned rather than boiled soft.
He enjoys greens with vinegar, pepper, and a small amount of salt.
He keeps a few hot sauces and adds them sparingly, preferring flavor and acidity over extreme heat.
His everyday cooking is mild to medium in spice because his wife has a lower tolerance for heat.
He likes trying international vegetarian food, including bean dishes, vegetable curries, noodles, and rice-based meals.
He is curious about unfamiliar ingredients but checks the price and whether they can be used in more than one meal.
He enjoys a good vegetable soup more than a complicated meat substitute designed to imitate a steak.
He does not especially like highly processed plant-based products when they are costly and taste strongly of additives.
He snacks on fruit, crackers, nuts when affordable, or whatever simple food is available after work.
He likes cookies but tries to keep them as an occasional treat rather than a nightly habit.
He drinks coffee, usually plain or with a modest amount of creamer, and is not fussy about the brand.
He drinks water during shifts and carries a reusable bottle when he remembers to fill it.
He prefers home-cooked meals to restaurant meals because he can control the ingredients and the cost.
He is willing to eat leftovers for lunch, provided they have been stored safely and still taste decent.
shopping_preferences: He makes most routine purchases online because the nearest range of stores is spread out and fuel costs add up.
He compares prices across more than one seller before buying anything that costs more than a small amount.
He reads reviews for recurring complaints, especially battery failures, poor delivery, and difficult returns.
He tends to favor low-cost or refurbished devices, though excitement about a new model can pull him toward an upgrade.
He uses store pickup when delivery fees are high or when a package might be left outside in bad weather.
He checks shipping estimates because rural delivery can be slower than the website's first estimate suggests.
He keeps screenshots or order emails until he is sure an item works and the return period has passed.
He buys groceries in person when fresh produce is important, but orders pantry staples online if the price and delivery are sensible.
He uses coupons and discount codes, yet an appealing deal can still lead him to purchase something he had not planned to buy.
He is wary of buy-now-pay-later offers but has used installment payments for a phone upgrade.
He avoids buying from unfamiliar sellers when the return policy is vague, even if the listing is cheaper.
He is more likely to spend on a tool or device if he can picture using it several times a week.
He looks for durable everyday items but does not always have enough upfront cash to choose the most durable option.
He buys clothes infrequently and usually chooses comfortable, plain items that are easy to wash.
He tries not to shop when he is tired late at night, but scrolling product pages in bed can weaken that intention.
health_and_wellness_preferences: He sees good health as something built from repeatable everyday habits rather than a single expensive program.
He wants preventive care, but appointment availability, transport, and potential bills affect how promptly he seeks it.
He values walking because it is free, easy to do near home, and does not require special equipment.
He prefers exercise that feels useful or enjoyable to a formal gym routine he has to pay for and drive to.
He tries to eat vegetables, beans, and fruit regularly without expecting every meal to be perfectly balanced.
He believes sleep matters and knows late-night browsing is one of the habits that interferes with it.
He appreciates meditation, prayer, breathing exercises, and journaling as low-cost ways to settle himself.
He wants health advice to account for shift work, limited money, and the fact that stress cannot always be removed.
attitude_to_new_products: He gets genuinely excited by new phones, useful apps, and small improvements in everyday technology.
He is willing to replace a device before it is unusable if a new version seems substantially more convenient.
He sometimes overestimates how much a new gadget will improve his daily routine.
He watches demonstrations and reads reviews before deciding, though excitement may still outrun his budget.
He enjoys showing his wife a feature he has discovered, even when she is less interested in upgrading.
He prefers products that work without extensive setup and can be repaired or returned locally or by mail.
He is skeptical of claims that an expensive product will transform health, productivity, or happiness.
After an impulsive purchase, he can admit that the older version would probably have been enough.
travel_preferences: He enjoys travel but needs to plan well ahead around work hours, car reliability, and household bills.
He has taken occasional international vacations rather than traveling every year, often because a family connection or group arrangement makes the trip possible.
He and his wife have visited Canada and Mexico; they remember the people, street scenes, and unfamiliar food more vividly than luxury amenities.
He prefers staying with relatives or in modest lodging rather than spending heavily on a resort.
He checks passport validity, transportation connections, medical access, and likely extra fees before booking.
He compares travel dates and routes online and is willing to accept a longer journey for a substantial saving.
He likes walking around a destination and observing ordinary neighborhood life rather than following a packed tour schedule.
He is curious about local vegetarian dishes and will ask politely about ingredients even when he is unsure of the language.
He enjoys the anticipation of planning almost as much as the trip itself, though he does not want to book something the household cannot afford.
He prefers traveling with his wife or a trusted small group and dislikes feeling responsible for a large party's schedule.

traits: Generally cheerful and enthusiastic, particularly when he is talking about a hands-on project, a good walk, a new app, or an upcoming plan.
Reserved in unfamiliar company and more comfortable in small groups than at crowded gatherings.
Warm and attentive with people he knows well, showing care through practical help rather than elaborate emotional speeches.
Reflective and inclined to replay difficult conversations privately before deciding what he thinks.
Hopeful by temperament, though his hope can coexist with a blunt awareness of bills, unstable work, and limited choices.
Resourceful about stretching food, maintaining inexpensive equipment, and finding a workable substitute when a plan falls through.
Curious about technology and global culture, even though he has to be careful about the cost of indulging those interests.
Skeptical of institutions and polished public messaging; he wants to know who benefits and who is expected to absorb the downside.
Patient with a beginner who is genuinely trying, but impatient with people who talk down to workers or treat service jobs as effortless.
More conscientious about food safety, church commitments, and keeping promises to loved ones than about paperwork or long-term financial tracking.
Prone to impulse purchases when a new phone or accessory seems unusually useful, followed by regret when the monthly payment appears.
Able to be stubborn once he feels someone is dismissing his lived experience, but willing to reconsider when a trusted person speaks plainly.
Not naturally confrontational; he often holds back in a tense moment and later wishes he had been more direct.
Socially loyal, with a small circle of close friends and a broader circle of familiar neighbors and congregation members.
Enjoys solitude without being isolated: a quiet walk or an evening tinkering at home can restore him, while prolonged loneliness weighs on him.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. Shane is interested in unfamiliar music, international places, practical technology, and new ways to solve everyday problems. He is open to experiences when they feel meaningful or useful, though he is not drawn to change for its own sake and remains attached to regional customs and familiar routines.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate and uneven. He is careful about hygiene, food handling, and commitments that affect other people. He can be disorganized with forms, budgets, and household paperwork, especially when several urgent expenses compete for attention. He wants to be more systematic but does not reliably sustain elaborate planning systems.
big_five.extraversion: Low to moderate. He is reflective and needs time alone, dislikes large noisy gatherings, and rarely seeks the spotlight. He can be warm, funny, and animated with his wife, close friends, or familiar church members, so his reserve is not a lack of social interest.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high. He is considerate, cooperative, and usually willing to help, but his agreeableness has limits. He becomes blunt when he thinks someone is exploiting a worker, dismissing a financial hardship, or confusing politeness with obedience.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. Financial uncertainty and late-night screen use can leave him keyed up, and he sometimes worries about health costs or whether his work hours will be cut. He generally recovers through prayer, quiet reflection, exercise, and talking with his wife rather than remaining distressed for long.

beliefs: Inflation is a very big problem because higher prices for groceries, fuel, utilities, and medicine leave little room in his household budget.
He experiences inflation as severe hardship, not as an abstract economic figure; a small increase in several essentials can erase the money he had set aside.
He rates the current economy as poor, even though he recognizes that some industries and households are doing well.
His family's financial situation feels about the same as it did four years ago: it has not collapsed, but it has not meaningfully improved either.
A full-time job should provide enough stability to plan ordinary life, though he knows his own work does not currently offer that security.
Small businesses and private enterprise can create useful products and local jobs when they have room to operate.
Competition can improve quality and lower prices, but it does not automatically protect people with little bargaining power.
He generally favors limited regulation, while accepting rules that prevent unsafe food, wage theft, fraud, or direct harm to workers and customers.
He is populist and anti-establishment in the sense that he distrusts concentrated power and wants ordinary people to have more say in decisions affecting them.
He is skeptical of both major parties and does not assume that politicians who use working-class language will actually serve working people.
He is wary of large corporations when they can shape rules, avoid accountability, or squeeze smaller suppliers and employees.
He thinks local businesses are valuable, but does not believe every local business owner is automatically fair or generous.
He is somewhat confident that elections are fair; he believes votes are generally counted through legitimate processes but worries about access, political pressure, and misleading claims.
He thinks election rules should be understandable and consistently applied, and dislikes claims of fraud that are made without credible evidence.
He believes people should be able to criticize government without being treated as disloyal.
He thinks practical cooperation across political lines matters more than winning every argument, although he admits he does not always practice that when he feels provoked.
He believes abortion should be legal in most cases, while regarding it as morally serious and emotionally complicated rather than an easy subject.
His Christian faith shapes his concern for compassion, forgiveness, and the dignity of people whose choices he may not personally share.
He believes congregations should care for neighbors in practical ways, not only speak about charity from a pulpit.
He does not think being religious makes someone automatically honest, kind, or wise.
He believes healthcare should be accessible before an illness becomes an emergency, and he is frustrated when cost delays ordinary care.
He favors mental-health support that is available without shaming people or assuming they can afford private treatment.
He thinks substance addiction is a serious community problem and sees treatment, family support, and accountability as more useful than contempt.
He regards food safety and fair treatment of kitchen workers as basic responsibilities, not special favors.
He believes a person can care about the environment without having money for premium products or a lifestyle built around expensive choices.
His vegetarian diet is a personal attempt to live according to his values, but he does not regard meat-eating relatives as people he needs to lecture.
He believes preventive health habits matter, while also recognizing that health is affected by work conditions, money, stress, and access to care.
He thinks physical activity should be practical and sustainable; a regular walk counts even if it is not part of a formal training plan.
He sees technology as useful when it solves a real problem, but suspects companies often encourage upgrades before people need them.
He enjoys global media and travel because they make the world feel wider than his immediate community, without making him ashamed of his local roots.
He believes local traditions are worth keeping when they help people care for one another, but should not be used to excuse cruelty or exclusion.
He thinks a family should be able to disagree privately without turning every difference into a test of loyalty.
He believes financial hardship is not proof of laziness or bad character; he also knows that habits and choices still matter within the limits people face.
He values privacy and does not think every personal struggle needs to be shared publicly on social media.
He thinks it is important to keep promises, but a person should be honest when changing circumstances make a promise impossible.
He believes travel can teach humility, especially when he is a visitor and does not understand the customs or history of a place.
He thinks a good life includes rest, close relationships, and useful work, not just income or status.
He believes optimism is worthwhile when it helps someone keep taking the next step, but not when it is used to deny real problems.
skills: Prepares vegetables, portions ingredients, and keeps a prep station orderly during busy service periods.
Understands basic food-safety practices, including clean surfaces, careful storage, date labeling, and avoiding cross-contamination.
Can keep several routine kitchen tasks moving while remaining aware of what needs to be ready next.
Knows how to adjust a simple recipe when an ingredient is missing, provided the substitution is practical and safe.
Can prepare filling vegetarian meals from inexpensive pantry staples without relying on complicated equipment.
Has practical repair ability with basic household tools and is willing to learn from a clear demonstration.
Can compare product listings, identify suspiciously incomplete specifications, and locate return-policy details online.
Uses a smartphone confidently for maps, messaging, social media, online shopping, photography, and workplace scheduling.
Can research a route and make a basic travel checklist for documents, cost, transport, and lodging.
Is a steady walker and knows how to pace himself on a long outing rather than exhausting himself early.
Can listen patiently to a friend who needs to talk, particularly when he does not feel expected to provide a perfect solution.
Is good at remembering practical details about people, such as a relative's appointment or a neighbor's ongoing repair problem.
Can work cooperatively with kitchen staff and usually avoids turning a minor disagreement into a public argument.
Has basic computer and email skills, though complicated spreadsheets and forms remain uncomfortable.
Can use prayer, measured breathing, and quiet reflection to bring down his immediate stress level.

relationships.name: Lydia Blevins
relationships.description: Lydia works intermittent part-time hours as a home-care aide. Their household income together is below $25,000 a year, and they share responsibility for bills, meals, transportation, and decisions about purchases. They are affectionate and loyal but can become tense when an unexpected expense collides with an already tight month. She is more cautious about device upgrades than Shane and often helps him pause before committing to an installment payment. He tries to protect her from worry by staying quiet about problems, which sometimes frustrates her more than an honest conversation would.

relationships.name: Megan Blevins
relationships.description: Megan lives separately and is building her own life, with occasional financial or practical support from her parents when they can manage it. Shane is proud of her independence and careful not to promise regular help that his income cannot sustain. Their calls are often brief and practical, but he likes hearing about her plans and will look up a route, repair, or job lead if she asks.

relationships.name: Caleb Morris
relationships.description: Caleb is a friend from the wider local community who shares Shane's interest in walking and occasional fishing. He is one of the few people Shane can sit with without having to keep a conversation constantly moving. Their plans are casual and often depend on weather, car availability, and work shifts.

relationships.name: Pastor Elaine Carter
relationships.description: Elaine knows Shane as a regular participant who is more comfortable helping with practical tasks than speaking in front of a group. He trusts her because she does not treat faith as a substitute for material help or claim every problem has an easy spiritual answer.

relationships.name: Rosa Martinez
relationships.description: Rosa works overlapping shifts in the hospital kitchen. They coordinate prep tasks and occasionally exchange inexpensive meal ideas. Shane respects her efficiency and feels comfortable asking her a direct question when he is unsure how a kitchen procedure has changed.

relationships.name: Denise Blevins
relationships.description: Denise lives within driving distance and is more financially stable than Shane. He feels grateful for her help but does not want their relationship to become a cycle of borrowing and repayment. She is also the relative most likely to remind him that a new phone is not an emergency.

occupation.title: Elementary-school student
occupation.organization: A public elementary school in Sacramento
occupation.description: Elliot is not employed and is not expected to participate in the labor force. His main responsibilities are attending school, completing age-appropriate homework, following household rules, and doing a few small chores such as putting away his shoes, feeding the cat with a reminder, and carrying his plate to the sink. These are family responsibilities, not paid work.

interests: Building LEGO vehicles, garages, and structures, especially when he can modify the design rather than follow every instruction.
Drawing imaginary maps with roads, rivers, neighborhoods, and labels for places that do not exist.
Playing Minecraft in a family-approved setting, mostly building houses, rail lines, and obstacle courses.
Playing age-appropriate games on a Nintendo Switch, especially platform, racing, and cooperative games.
Basketball at school or at the park, where he enjoys shooting baskets more than formal drills.
Watching Sacramento Kings highlights with his father, even though he does not follow every player or statistic.
Reading illustrated books, funny chapter books, graphic novels, and nonfiction books with clear diagrams.
Learning facts about space, animals, bridges, weather, and machines when the information is presented visually.
Watching nature and science videos with a parent nearby, then repeating one or two facts at dinner.
Making paper airplanes and testing which ones fly farthest in a safe open space.
Board and card games that are short enough to play in one sitting.
Going to a neighborhood park with his sister or a friend.
Drawing comic panels, usually with a hero, a problem, and a silly ending.
Listening to upbeat pop, movie soundtracks, and songs his parents play in the car.
Visiting the library, especially when he can choose books himself.
Small hands-on experiments, such as testing which household objects float, with adult supervision.
Looking at maps and asking how long a trip would take by car.
Watching animation and family comedies, including episodes he has already seen.
Helping with simple cooking tasks when they involve stirring, measuring, or arranging toppings.
Collecting a few small toys and cards, though he does not maintain a carefully organized collection.
likes: Crispy chicken, rice, buttered noodles, cheese pizza, and tacos with familiar fillings.
Mild food with sauces on the side so he can decide whether to use them.
Strawberries, watermelon, and seedless grapes when they are washed and ready to eat.
Chocolate-chip cookies as an occasional treat, especially warm ones shared at home.
Breakfast on weekends when nobody is rushing him out the door.
A small amount of salsa if it is not too hot and he can try it before putting it on his food.
Eating outside at a picnic table when the weather is pleasant and there are no too many insects.
Stores where he can see the item in person before his parents decide whether to buy it.
Being given two reasonable choices instead of being asked an open-ended question while distracted.
New toys or games when a friend has already explained how they work.
Bright colors for art supplies and dark blue or green for clothes.
A soft hoodie and sneakers that do not pinch or need frequent adjustment.
Having a predictable plan for the school morning.
Building something with a clear purpose, such as a ramp, bridge, or vehicle.
When adults notice effort rather than only pointing out mistakes.
The cat sleeping near him, as long as it does not sit on the project he is building.
Short car trips with a playlist he can help choose.
Air-conditioned rooms during Sacramento's hottest summer afternoons.
Being allowed to explain his side before a parent decides what happened.
A bedtime story or a few pages of reading together when he is not already overtired.
dislikes: Very spicy food, especially when the heat lingers after he has stopped eating.
Mixed-texture foods where a soft and crunchy ingredient are combined unexpectedly.
Mushrooms and cooked spinach, which he usually tries to avoid rather than argue about.
Being rushed while tying his shoes or finishing breakfast.
Losing a game because someone changed a rule halfway through.
Being teased about a mistake in front of other children.
Long stretches of handwriting without a chance to move or take a short break.
Loud hand dryers, sudden alarms, and crowded indoor spaces that echo.
An itchy clothing tag or socks that have slipped out of place.
Having a project taken apart before he has had a chance to show it to someone.
When his younger sister touches a build and then says she did not touch it.
Being told 'because I said so' when he believes he has asked a fair question.
A surprise change of plans after he has pictured how the day will go.
Long shopping trips with no clear end point.
Being expected to entertain himself in a waiting room without anything to read or draw.
Very hot weather when he has to walk outside or play in direct sun.
Movies with prolonged peril or frightening scenes that are difficult to stop thinking about at bedtime.
Having to share a favorite treat before he has decided whether he is finished.
Being compared with a classmate who is faster at schoolwork or sports.
A tablet or game being turned off without a warning when time is nearly up.
culinary_tastes: His usual food preferences are familiar and mild rather than adventurous, though he occasionally wants to taste a small bite of something new.
He likes Mexican-American family meals such as tacos and quesadillas when the ingredients are separated and the salsa is optional.
He prefers chicken, eggs, beans, and cheese over strongly flavored or heavily seasoned meat.
He will eat rice with a simple topping and sometimes asks for it plain.
He likes noodles but is not enthusiastic about complicated sauces.
He accepts vegetables more readily when they are crunchy, served separately, or included in a food he already likes.
He is more willing to eat fruit when it is cut into manageable pieces.
He enjoys restaurant meals as a treat but does not want every meal to be unfamiliar.
He likes deciding whether to add ketchup, mild salsa, or cheese after the main food is served.
He does not think much about organic versus conventional food; that is a parent-level shopping decision.
He can be persuaded to try one bite without promising to finish a full serving.
He is learning that a food can taste different depending on how it is cooked, but he may still reject it by appearance.
shopping_and_products: Elliot does not shop independently and has no personal budget beyond occasional small allowances or gift money managed with his parents.
Most groceries are bought by a parent, and he sometimes comes along to choose one snack or help find items on a list.
He prefers seeing toys, shoes, and sports equipment in a store because he can handle them and check their size.
He enjoys browsing the toy or book aisle more than shopping for household supplies.
Online purchases are made by his parents; he may point out an item but needs adult permission and supervision.
He is attracted to colorful packaging and recognizable game characters, but interest does not guarantee that he gets the product.
He tends to become enthusiastic about a new game after seeing a friend use it, then may lose interest after the novelty wears off.
He is skeptical of unfamiliar foods but less skeptical of a new art pen, building set, or game with a clear demonstration.
He can compare simple features, such as whether a ball feels grippy or a toy has the pieces he wants, but is not responsible for evaluating price or quality.
He understands that parents sometimes say a product costs too much, but does not yet grasp household budgeting in detail.
travel_and_lifestyle: He is most comfortable with local outings and short drives, especially when he knows where the family is going.
He enjoys trips to parks, libraries, museums with interactive exhibits, and relatives' homes.
He has taken family trips within California, including visits to the coast, but is not a frequent or independent traveler.
Long drives become difficult if he is bored, hungry, or unable to see how much longer the trip will take.
He likes travel better when he can bring a book, headphones, or a small building toy.
He is curious about other places but has only a child's picture of international travel, shaped by books, family stories, and media.
His lifestyle is a mix of school, screen time, indoor projects, and bursts of outdoor play rather than a highly scheduled sports routine.
He prefers an active afternoon with a friend to a formal class that requires sustained practice, though he can enjoy a class once he feels comfortable.
He likes family outings but also enjoys having an ordinary weekend at home.
He needs adult help with sun protection, hydration, transportation, safety, and decisions about activities.

traits: Curious about how ordinary things work, particularly wheels, bridges, game mechanics, and household devices.
Imaginative, especially when drawing maps, making up characters, or combining unrelated LEGO pieces into a vehicle.
Sociable in familiar settings, but slower to warm up when a group of older children is already established.
Competitive during basketball, card games, and video games; he dislikes losing more when he thinks the rules were unclear.
Affectionate toward family and familiar pets, although he does not always want to stop what he is doing to show it.
Fairness-minded in a concrete, immediate way: he cares strongly about whose turn it is and whether the same rule applies to everyone.
Sometimes impatient with tasks that feel repetitive, especially copying, tidying, or redoing work he considers already finished.
Proud of skills he has practiced and sensitive to being corrected in front of classmates.
Generally cheerful, with ordinary fluctuations; a disappointing game or a rushed morning can make him grumpy for a while.
Capable of apologizing after cooling down, but may first insist that the other person started it.
Easily drawn toward screens and snacks when he is bored, and less likely to notice time passing without adult limits.
Cautious about unfamiliar food and new group activities, but willing to try them when a trusted friend or adult joins him.
More persistent with self-chosen projects than with assigned work; he may return to a half-built construction several days later.
Somewhat distractible when there is conversation or movement nearby, but can concentrate for a long time on a favorite game or construction.
Kind in small practical ways, such as saving a seat for a friend or helping his sister find a missing toy, without thinking of himself as especially generous.

big_five.openness: Moderately high for his age. He enjoys inventing stories, learning surprising facts, and trying a new game, but prefers familiar routines and familiar foods when he is tired.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate to low in independent organization, which is developmentally ordinary. He can follow a clear checklist and takes pride in finishing a project, but needs reminders about belongings, time, and homework.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate. He likes playing with a few friends and talking about his interests, but can become quiet in a large unfamiliar group and needs some downtime after a busy day.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderately high but uneven under pressure. He is often cooperative and affectionate, yet can become stubborn when he thinks someone has skipped a turn or blamed him unfairly.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. He is not persistently anxious, but worries about being laughed at, tests, getting in trouble, and sudden changes to plans; reassurance and a clear explanation usually help.

beliefs: He believes rules should be the same for everyone, although he sometimes thinks a rule is fairer when it benefits him.
He believes people should get another chance after a mistake if they admit what happened.
He thinks adults should listen to a child's explanation before deciding who is in trouble.
He believes his parents usually know more about safety than he does, even when he dislikes their limits.
He thinks asking questions is a good way to learn, but can feel embarrassed if he asks one that classmates already know.
He believes school is important because children need to learn to read, do math, and figure things out.
He does not yet have a settled idea of what kind of adult he will become.
He thinks a person can be good at drawing and still need help with writing.
He believes practice helps with basketball and games, though he sometimes expects improvement to happen quickly.
He thinks winning is exciting but that a game is not fun when someone changes the rules to make sure they win.
He believes friends should include someone who is alone, but may hesitate if he fears the group will reject him too.
He thinks teasing can stop being funny when the person being teased asks for it to stop.
He believes his younger sister can be annoying and still deserve help when she is genuinely hurt.
He thinks pets need food, water, and gentle handling, even though he sometimes needs reminders about his own pet-care chores.
He believes food can be healthy and still taste good, but he does not want every meal to be a lesson about nutrition.
He thinks treats are more enjoyable when they are occasional rather than part of every meal.
He understands that his parents work to pay for the family's home and necessities, though he does not understand their full financial responsibilities.
He believes a toy or game is not automatically worth buying just because an advertisement makes it look exciting.
He sometimes believes that a new game will be the best one ever, then revises that opinion after playing it.
He thinks people should take care of parks because everyone uses them and litter makes them unpleasant.
He has a basic idea that wasting water is not good, partly because he has heard adults talk about dry summers in California.
He believes the weather can be dangerous when it is extremely hot and that adults are right to remind him to drink water.
He knows that not everyone has the same home, family, food, or money, but he is still learning what those differences mean.
He thinks people can have different favorite foods, holidays, or languages without one family being wrong.
He recognizes Christmas as an important family holiday but does not express a strong personal religious commitment.
He believes news stories can be confusing and usually asks an adult when he hears a serious topic he does not understand.
He has heard his parents discuss prices and healthcare, but those are not developed political positions of his own.
He thinks a phone or tablet can be useful for talking, learning, and games, but also knows it can make bedtime harder.
He believes people should not share a classmate's private messages or embarrassing pictures without permission.
He thinks a new product might be fun, but wants to know how it works before trying something that seems strange or unsafe.
He believes traveling can be exciting, but also thinks home is comfortable and does not need to be left every weekend.
He sees exercise as something that can be fun when it means basketball or running around, not as a grown-up health rule.
He believes being wrong is not the same as being stupid, even if he sometimes feels that way in the moment.
He thinks adults do not always know exactly what children are thinking and that it helps when he explains rather than expects them to guess.
skills: Reads age-appropriate chapter books and graphic novels independently, though he may choose a shorter book when tired.
Can explain the basic rules of his favorite games and remember details about a game world or story.
Builds multi-part LEGO designs and modifies them when a structure does not work as expected.
Draws clear maps and simple comic panels, with more enthusiasm for ideas and labels than polished technique.
Has basic multiplication and measurement skills and can follow a recipe step when an adult supervises.
Can use a tablet or game console for familiar age-appropriate activities, with parental controls and time limits.
Can make simple snacks, pour water, pack a few school items, and tidy a small area when given a clear reminder.
Can ride a bicycle on familiar paths with appropriate adult permission and supervision.
Recognizes when a friend is disappointed and can offer a practical gesture of support, though he may not know what to say.
Is learning to pause and explain what happened during a disagreement rather than immediately insisting that he is right.

relationships.name: Claire Graham
relationships.description: Claire is a pediatric physical therapist. She is warm and attentive but often has a busy work schedule. She checks Elliot's homework and notices when he is unusually quiet. He goes to her first when he is worried or embarrassed, though he sometimes finds her reminders about water, sunscreen, and bedtime repetitive.

relationships.name: Daniel Graham
relationships.description: Daniel is a civil engineer for a county water utility. He likes practical explanations and often answers Elliot's questions about bridges, pipes, roads, and how buildings stay up. He watches basketball with him and encourages him to try again after a missed shot, while sometimes being too quick to offer a solution when Elliot wants to finish telling the story.

relationships.name: Maya Graham
relationships.description: Maya is in second grade. Elliot loves her and occasionally helps her with a game or a missing object, but he gets annoyed when she touches an unfinished build or copies his jokes. Their disagreements are usually ordinary sibling disputes and are settled with adult help or a compromise.

relationships.name: Noah
relationships.description: Noah is one of Elliot's regular recess companions. They talk about games and basketball and sometimes compete over who can make a shot. Elliot is comfortable being silly with him but worries that Noah will laugh if he shows something he has drawn and is not sure about.

relationships.name: Ms. Patel
relationships.description: Ms. Patel gives Elliot clear, step-by-step directions and encourages him to check his written work. He respects her, though he can feel singled out if she corrects him in front of the whole class. He responds better when she explains what to improve rather than simply saying to try harder.

relationships.name: Grandmother Linda
relationships.description: Linda lives elsewhere in California and visits several times a year. She shares family stories, sends books for birthdays, and lets the children help with simple cooking. Elliot enjoys hearing stories about his father's childhood, even when he has heard the same one before.

occupation.title: High-school student; no paid employment
occupation.organization: Milwaukee public high school
occupation.description: School is Nolan's main responsibility. He attends classes, completes assignments, and occasionally helps with school event setup through the media or stage-crew activities. He is not seeking a job and is not expected to participate in the labor force; his parents want him to focus on graduating. At home he does ordinary chores, such as taking out recycling and helping carry groceries, but these are family responsibilities rather than employment. He has no work supervisor, professional credentials, or adult career expertise.

interests: Console video games, especially story-driven games and cooperative games he can play with friends.
Watching short comedy clips and game videos online.
Basketball at the park or recreation center, more for the social part than for serious competition.
The Milwaukee Bucks and occasional NBA highlights, though he is not a statistics-focused fan.
Movies with memorable characters, clever dialogue, or a good soundtrack.
Horror movies with friends, provided they are more fun than relentlessly disturbing.
Music playlists that move between hip-hop, alternative rock, pop, and older songs his parents play in the car.
Editing short video clips for school projects or just to make a friend laugh.
Trying out new snacks or drinks when friends recommend them.
Walking around local shops with a friend when neither of them has a specific plan.
Watching repair, cooking, or behind-the-scenes videos without necessarily attempting the project himself.
Casual photography on his phone, especially unusual signs, street scenes, and pets.
Board and party games when the group is small enough that everyone gets a turn.
Listening to friends talk about things he has not tried, even if he does not always join in.
Looking at used electronics and game listings to compare prices.
Local festivals and neighborhood events when a friend or family member is already going.
Stories about how cities, sports teams, or entertainment industries changed over time.
Cooking simple food with his mother when he is in the mood and there is no time pressure.
likes: A cheeseburger with a crisp edge, pickles, and a manageable amount of sauce.
Tacos with grilled chicken, beans, or ground beef, plus salsa that has some flavor but is not painfully hot.
Thin-crust pizza, especially reheated leftovers that are still crisp underneath.
Breakfast sandwiches when someone else is already making or buying them.
Chocolate-chip cookies, particularly warm ones, and ordinary packaged cookies as an easy snack.
A bowl of cereal late at night, even though he knows it is not a particularly balanced meal.
Macaroni and cheese as comfort food, with no strong preference for elaborate versions.
Trying a new restaurant if a friend can explain what to order and the prices are visible.
Cold drinks with lots of ice in summer and hot chocolate when it is cold out.
A familiar neighborhood diner or casual restaurant where he does not have to dress up.
Comfortable hoodies, clean sneakers, and clothes that do not require careful coordination.
Buying a game used if the case and disc are in good condition.
A quiet seat near the edge of a room rather than being squeezed into the middle of a crowd.
Having a clear plan for a ride home, even when the rest of the outing is spontaneous.
Music playing softly while he does a repetitive task.
People who explain a rule or correction without making it sound like a personal insult.
A short, funny conversation that does not become a debate about everything.
Dogs, especially friendly dogs who approach without jumping all over him.
A mild spring or fall day when he can walk without being too hot or cold.
Finding a surprisingly good item at a thrift store or a used-game shop.
Watching a movie with friends and then talking about the best or dumbest parts afterward.
A day with one or two obligations and enough unstructured time to do what he wants.
dislikes: Food so spicy that he cannot taste anything else.
Mushy vegetables or fruit that has gone soft in a way he was not expecting.
Being told to try something new while people watch and wait for his reaction.
Adults who dismiss a concern with “you'll understand when you're older.”
Being asked several questions in a row when he has only just walked in the door.
Long, forced family conversations where everyone has to take turns reporting on their life.
Group projects in which one person does nearly all the work and another takes equal credit.
School assignments with unclear instructions and a strict deadline that was mentioned only once.
People who play videos aloud on a phone in a quiet public place.
Being teased in front of someone he wants to impress.
Crowded shops when he is tired or hungry.
Expensive clothing that seems to be priced mainly for its logo.
Being pressured to buy something immediately because it is supposedly the last chance.
Long car rides without a chance to stretch or choose the music.
Very formal restaurants where he is unsure about the expected behavior.
Moralizing lectures about screen time that ignore why he is using his phone.
Having a friend share a private message or embarrassing photo without asking.
Cleaning a mess that someone else could have prevented.
Strong artificial fruit flavors in candy or drinks.
People who treat every disagreement as proof that the other person is stupid or evil.
preferences.culinary_tastes: He is a meat-eater with a familiar comfort-food base, but he is not opposed to vegetarian meals when they are filling and taste good. His preferred spice level is mild to medium: salsa, pepper, and a little hot sauce are welcome, while extreme heat feels like a dare rather than a flavor. He is willing to try a new cuisine when the setting is casual and a friend can recommend an approachable dish. He is less adventurous when he is hungry, rushed, or paying with money he saved himself. He likes a mix of home-cooked meals and inexpensive takeout, and he does not think of food as a major hobby. He will eat vegetables more readily when they are roasted, included in tacos, or served with something familiar than when they are presented as a plain side.
preferences.shopping_habits: He shops occasionally rather than for entertainment every week. Most clothing and household purchases are handled by his parents, while he uses saved gift money or allowance for games, snacks, and small accessories. He checks prices online and is willing to buy used games or electronics, but can make an impulsive small purchase when a friend recommends it or a sale appears. He prefers seeing shoes and clothes in person because fit matters, while ordering a known game or cable online feels easy. He is not a coupon expert, but he notices shipping costs and dislikes paying more for a logo.
preferences.health_consciousness: He has a moderate, inconsistent interest in health. He understands basic advice about sleep, activity, and balanced meals, but he does not plan his life around it. He likes walking and recreational basketball, drinks water when reminded, and sometimes chooses fruit or a sandwich; he also snacks late, eats convenience food, and stays up gaming. Organic labels do not strongly influence him, and he is more persuaded by taste, price, and whether food seems fresh.
preferences.attitude_toward_new_products: He is cautiously curious. He will try a new game, snack, or inexpensive gadget if someone he trusts recommends it, but he avoids buying expensive products just because an advertisement calls them revolutionary. He likes comparing reviews and watching a short demonstration, and he can be skeptical of influencer endorsements that sound rehearsed.
preferences.travel_habits: He is not a frequent traveler. Most trips are family visits, day outings, or domestic vacations reached by car; he has limited experience with international travel. He enjoys a change of scenery once he is there but is not fond of complicated itineraries, early departures, or uncertain transportation. He would like to visit a large city outside the Midwest with a friend or relative, but prefers having a clear place to stay and a way home.
preferences.cultural_background: His everyday cultural reference points are local Milwaukee life, public school, family routines, sports, American popular media, and a broad online world. The German and Polish parts of his family history come up in stories from grandparents and a few food traditions, but he does not speak either language or treat ancestry as a complete description of who he is. Friends and classmates have exposed him to different foods and customs, and he is interested when people share them without being treated as spokespeople for an entire group.
preferences.lifestyle: His lifestyle is urban and family-centered rather than independent. He walks or takes the bus for familiar nearby trips, relies on his parents for longer rides, and spends substantial leisure time at home on screens. He is neither especially minimalist nor extravagant: he keeps a few things he cares about, accumulates game cases and cables, and does not mind ordinary clutter until it interferes with finding something. He gets periodic activity from walking and casual basketball, but does not follow a structured fitness program.

traits: He is curious about how things are made and how a story or game is put together, though he does not seek novelty in every part of his life.
He has a wry, sometimes self-deprecating sense of humor and uses jokes to reduce awkwardness.
He is observant about social dynamics and can tell when a friend is being left out, but he does not always know how to intervene.
He is loyal to a small circle and more reserved with people he does not know.
He can be stubborn when he thinks an adult is treating him as incapable simply because he is young.
He is not naturally organized; reminders and visible deadlines help him more than plans he makes and then forgets.
He cares what his friends think, even while insisting that he does not care about popularity.
He is more compassionate in one-to-one situations than he is comfortable being in a public, emotionally exposed moment.
He gets defensive when criticized in a vague or mocking way, but can accept specific advice from someone he trusts.
He enjoys having a choice and tends to resist instructions that seem arbitrary.
He can be patient with a game, a device, or a creative task that interests him, but impatient with repetitive chores.
He is generally hopeful about his own future in brief flashes, then becomes uncertain when asked to make a concrete plan.
He avoids serious arguments when possible, sometimes leaving a conversation rather than saying what is bothering him.
He is neither especially competitive nor indifferent; he likes winning, but dislikes being made to feel foolish in public.
He is comfortable with people whose backgrounds differ from his own, though his knowledge of other cultures is uneven and mostly comes from school, friends, food, and media.

big_five.openness: Moderately high. He is interested in music, film, game design, new cuisines, and different ways people live, but often prefers familiar routines and proven entertainment when tired.
big_five.conscientiousness: Low to moderate. He can be dependable when another person is counting on him, yet he procrastinates, misplaces small items, and underestimates how long assignments will take.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate-low. He enjoys a few friends, group jokes, and occasional school events, but does not need to be the center of attention and needs quiet time after a crowded day.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate to high. He is usually considerate and dislikes cruelty, but can be sarcastic, prickly, or unhelpful when he feels nagged or patronized.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate. He has ordinary adolescent worries about school, friendships, and what comes next; stress tends to show up as avoidance, irritability, or staying up too late rather than dramatic outbursts.

beliefs: Finishing high school matters because it keeps options open, even if a diploma does not automatically solve everything.
A four-year college is not the only respectable route, and practical training can be a sensible choice when it leads to real skills.
Taking on a large loan without a clear plan is risky; he has not yet worked out what amount of debt might be worthwhile.
Adults should explain rules and consequences instead of expecting young people to obey simply because they are older.
Parents can set reasonable limits, but teenagers should gradually be trusted with decisions that affect them.
It is unfair to judge a person by one mistake when there is a pattern of how they treat people.
Being funny is not an excuse to keep humiliating someone after they have made it clear they are hurt.
Friendship is shown more by checking in and showing up than by saying dramatic things in a group chat.
People should be able to change their mind without being mocked for what they used to believe.
He does not assume a person is telling the whole story just because they sound confident online.
Social media can help people stay connected, but it makes it too easy to compare ordinary life with someone else's best moments.
A phone is useful and entertaining, but it can also steal time he meant to spend sleeping or finishing schoolwork.
People deserve privacy in their messages and photos; sharing something private for laughs can permanently damage trust.
A person should not have to be an expert on every political issue before having a reasonable opinion about it.
He is not attached to a political party and is wary of politicians who make every disagreement sound like an emergency.
He thinks government should help people access basic services, including health care, but is unsure how to pay for every proposal or how well institutions would manage it.
Medical care should not become impossible to afford when someone gets sick, though he has little personal experience with insurance details.
Gun violence is frightening and feels like a real problem, especially when it affects schools and public places; he is still learning about which policies work.
People should be able to own firearms legally, but he sees a difference between that and having no safeguards at all.
Climate change seems real and worth addressing, even though online arguments about it can make the subject feel exhausting.
People moving to the United States should be treated humanely, and rules should be understandable; he does not have a developed view of every immigration policy.
Inflation and higher prices matter because his parents talk about grocery and household costs, even though he does not manage the family budget.
A job should pay enough to live on, but he has not yet learned what different jobs actually demand day to day.
Hard work helps, but people do not all begin with the same money, support, safety, or opportunities.
Religion can be important to people without being something everyone has to share.
He is not sure whether he believes in God; his family has Catholic roots, but he does not currently practice in a committed way.
Family is important, but loving relatives does not mean every disagreement has to be ignored.
Trying food or listening to music from another culture is a good way to be curious, but it does not make him an authority on that culture.
Local neighborhoods need parks, safe sidewalks, and places for teenagers to spend time without being expected to buy something.
Being healthy is more than having a certain appearance, and he dislikes jokes that treat someone's body as public property.
Sleep makes a noticeable difference to his patience and concentration, even though he still stays up later than he intends.
A product being new or expensive does not automatically make it better; it should work and be worth the money.
Fairness does not always mean everyone gets exactly the same thing; sometimes people need different kinds of help.
He believes people should be able to disagree about politics without turning every relationship into a loyalty test.
He is worried by political hostility and public violence, but is not certain how much any one person can influence national events.
Voting will matter when he is old enough, but he wants to learn enough to make a choice rather than repeat his parents' preferences.
skills: Can use common phone, computer, and console interfaces without much assistance.
Can trim video clips, add basic captions, and assemble a simple school presentation.
