Has a good eye for when a video or image feels awkwardly edited, even if he cannot always explain the technical reason.
Can find product reviews and compare basic prices, though he sometimes gives too much weight to a confident-sounding online reviewer.
Knows how to navigate familiar Milwaukee bus routes and check arrival information on his phone.
Can make a few basic meals, including eggs, grilled cheese, boxed pasta, and simple tacos, with reminders to clean up afterward.
Is reasonably good at explaining a game or app to a friend who is new to it.
Can read a room and notice when a joke has gone too far, though he may wait for someone else to say so.
Has basic basketball skills and understands the rules well enough for casual play.
Can handle everyday chores such as recycling, carrying groceries, and loading a dishwasher, but is not consistently self-starting.
Has ordinary high-school computer literacy and does not have professional technical, financial, medical, or research expertise.

relationships.name: Laura Becker
relationships.description: Works as a clinic scheduling coordinator. She is organized and remembers school dates, permission forms, and appointments better than Nolan does. They are affectionate but sometimes clash over homework, phone use, and his habit of answering requests with “in a minute.” She is usually the parent he approaches when he wants practical advice.

relationships.name: Mark Becker
relationships.description: Works in maintenance for a municipal water utility. He is steady and practical, likes local sports, and is more comfortable showing care by doing something useful than by having a long emotional conversation. He encourages Nolan to learn to drive and consider a trade or technical program, while trying not to force a decision.

relationships.name: Grace Becker
relationships.description: A middle-school student who shares the house and sometimes borrows his chargers without asking. Nolan complains about her noise but is protective when other people make fun of her. They can spend an enjoyable hour gaming or watching clips together, then argue over whose turn it is.

relationships.name: Eli
relationships.description: A friend from school who shares Nolan's interest in games and comedy videos. Eli is more outgoing and often suggests plans; Nolan usually appreciates the invitation even when he pretends it is no big deal. They tease each other, but Nolan trusts him not to share private messages.

relationships.name: Maya
relationships.description: A perceptive friend from a group project and the school's media activities. She is comfortable asking direct questions, which sometimes makes Nolan deflect with a joke. He respects her opinions and will listen when she points out that he is procrastinating or being unfair.

relationships.name: Mrs. Alvarez
relationships.description: A teacher whose class Nolan enjoys because she connects events to people and daily life. He is more willing to ask her questions than most teachers because she gives specific feedback instead of treating mistakes as a character flaw.

relationships.name: Ron and Diane Becker
relationships.description: They live within driving distance and see the family for some holidays and birthdays. Ron tells stories about the family's Polish-American relatives, while Diane is more likely to talk about recipes and old neighborhood changes. Nolan likes them, though he can get restless during long visits.

occupation.title: Regional Grants Compliance Officer
occupation.organization: A long-established nonprofit community health network headquartered in Providence, Rhode Island.
occupation.employment_status: Permanent employee in a stable position with employer-sponsored benefits and a realistic path to expanded responsibilities. She currently works an approved reduced schedule of about 12 paid hours per week under a phased-return arrangement related to her household caregiving situation.
occupation.compensation_and_household_context: Her position has a competitive full-time-equivalent salary of approximately $76,000 a year. At her current 0.3 schedule, her gross wages are about $22,800 for the year, which is also the household's current annual cash income. Her husband has no current wage income while recovering from a back injury and awaiting a benefits decision. The employer has temporarily preserved her health benefits under its phased-return policy, but their budget remains extremely tight.
occupation.description: Kathleen tracks requirements and deadlines for a portfolio of state and federal grants that fund community health programs. She checks that expenses are documented properly, helps clinic managers prepare for audits, flags missed reporting deadlines, and explains grant rules in plain language to staff who do not work with financial compliance every day. Though she has reduced hours, she remains the person who understands the history of several complicated grants and is trusted to spot discrepancies before they become formal findings. She works in concentrated blocks, often remotely, and visits partner clinics around Rhode Island and neighboring states two or three times in a typical month. She is good at keeping calm when a deadline or audit issue becomes urgent, but her limited schedule means she has to be explicit about what she can and cannot take on. Her supervisor has discussed a gradual increase in hours and, eventually, a senior program-management role if her household circumstances permit.

interests: She enjoys small board-game gatherings where conversation matters as much as winning, particularly games that can be explained quickly and played around a kitchen table.
She likes socializing in familiar settings such as a parish hall, a friend's apartment, or a quiet diner rather than a crowded bar or a large formal event.
She reads library books, especially family stories, local history, biographies, and accessible nonfiction about American institutions.
She follows local news more closely than national political commentary and often checks whether a story affects a neighborhood service or a familiar workplace.
She likes walking for errands and short evening loops, especially when she can take a route with trees, old houses, or a view of the water.
She enjoys visiting neighborhood bakeries and small diners, though cost and her restricted diet mean she often buys only coffee or one modest item.
She is interested in practical public-health work and likes hearing how a clinic's services have helped a specific person.
She enjoys oral histories and family stories, especially accounts of how relatives managed work, illness, and housing in earlier generations.
She follows women's basketball and watches occasional local or college games with her husband when he is comfortable sitting for a while.
She likes televised courtroom dramas and older detective series, partly because she can follow them without needing to keep up with a subscription service.
She participates in a monthly board-game evening organized by two parish friends, though she sometimes has to cancel when work travel or caregiving intervenes.
She enjoys listening to a local radio station during household chores because the familiar voices make the apartment feel less quiet.
She is curious about how food traditions travel through families, even though she herself keeps a limited, repetitive menu.
She likes arranging practical neighborhood help, such as rides to appointments, meal drop-offs, or sharing information about a benefits office.
She sometimes works through crossword puzzles in a free newspaper and enjoys getting a difficult clue without looking it up.
She enjoys people-watching in a public park or at a bus stop, mostly noticing how people adapt to weather, errands, and small inconveniences.
She is interested in old buildings and local street names, especially when a friend explains the history without turning it into a lecture.
She likes the feeling of finishing a concrete task, such as closing a grant report or sorting a stack of bills, more than open-ended hobbies.
She is fond of quiet celebrations with family, where people bring ordinary food and nobody is expected to spend much.
She likes being useful to younger colleagues by showing them how to document decisions and avoid preventable grant mistakes.
likes: A calm kitchen table where people can sit for an hour without needing to buy another round or move along.
A short, specific meeting agenda and a written record of who agreed to do what.
People who explain a complicated rule in plain English and admit when they do not know the answer.
Reliable secondhand furniture that is plain, sturdy, and easy to repair.
Walking to a grocery store when the weather is mild and she has time to avoid using the car.
A well-worn paperback that can be borrowed from the library rather than purchased.
Mild flavors and familiar textures, especially oatmeal, toast, lentil soup, eggs, potatoes, and plain rice.
A strong cup of black tea in the morning and decaffeinated tea later in the evening.
A clean but not overly scented home; she prefers open windows to candles or plug-in fragrances.
Her parish's low-key community meals, where nobody makes a show of who brought what.
A friend who can disagree with her without humiliating her or demanding that she immediately change her mind.
Public libraries, bus routes, clinics, and other services that are genuinely accessible to people without a car.
Knowing the same shopkeepers and being recognized without being pressured into a long conversation.
A clear envelope system for rent, utilities, groceries, and transportation money.
Simple clothes in dark or neutral colors that can be washed easily and worn for several years.
Board games with modest rules and a little strategy, especially when the group is more interested in company than competition.
A supervisor who respects her limited schedule and gives her real responsibility rather than only assigning busywork.
Walking near the harbor or along a quiet neighborhood street without needing to turn the outing into exercise performance.
Family photographs and handwritten recipe cards, even though she rarely cooks the more elaborate dishes.
Small signs that someone has followed through, such as a clinic manager sending the missing receipt or a friend remembering an appointment.
dislikes: Being told that an app or device is simple when it requires multiple passwords, updates, and verification codes.
Salespeople who use urgency or fear to push a purchase she has not had time to compare.
Online-only forms for essential services, especially when a person cannot easily reach a real employee for help.
Food with strong heat, complicated sauces, or unexpected textures.
Large portions that make her feel wasteful or pressured to eat past her appetite.
Crowded restaurants with loud music, hard chairs, and a long wait for a basic meal.
Being asked to spend money socially just to prove that she cares about someone.
Corporate language that presents a cost-cutting decision as an exciting innovation.
People who confuse confidence with expertise or dismiss questions as ignorance.
A crowded apartment full of decorative objects that need dusting and have no practical use.
Replacing a usable household item simply because a newer model has appeared.
Unannounced changes to a work system shortly before a reporting deadline.
Long national political panels where guests talk over one another but offer no concrete plan.
Being described as naturally suited to caregiving, as if her time and energy do not count.
Perfume, strongly scented cleaning products, and air fresheners that linger in a small room.
Late-night phone notifications, especially messages that could easily have waited until morning.
People who treat lower-income families as careless rather than acknowledging the constraints of rent, medical bills, and transportation.
A flimsy product marketed as a premium or environmentally responsible purchase.
Having to make a private health or financial matter public in order to qualify for assistance.
Unnecessary travel for meetings that could have been handled with a clear call or a short written update.

culinary_tastes.overall_pattern: Her food choices are narrow, mild, and strongly shaped by cost, reflux, limited appetite, and a preference for predictable textures. She is not formally vegetarian, but meat is infrequent because it is expensive and she does not particularly miss it.
usual_foods: She commonly eats oatmeal, peanut-butter toast, eggs, plain rice, potatoes, lentils, canned beans, and simple vegetable soup.
She buys chicken or canned tuna when they are on sale, but does not plan elaborate meals around meat.
She is comfortable eating the same breakfast or lunch several days in a row if it is affordable and easy to prepare.
She favors soft, familiar foods and is wary of dishes with several mixed textures or ingredients she cannot identify.
She avoids very spicy food and rich sauces because they aggravate reflux.
She has some lactose sensitivity and usually chooses lactose-free milk or skips dairy rather than testing her luck.
She likes plain crackers, applesauce, and bananas as inexpensive snacks, though she sometimes relies on cookies when tired.
She appreciates a traditional holiday meal, such as a modest shepherd's pie or roast chicken, but does not cook a large feast herself.
She wants to eat more vegetables and regular meals, but fresh produce can be hard to use before it spoils when her schedule changes.
She is more likely to accept a new dish if a trusted family member explains what is in it and offers a small portion.

shopping_habits.pattern: Kathleen dislikes discretionary shopping and minimizes it, but she shops deliberately for necessities. She prefers an in-person store where she can compare prices and inspect an item, and her limited broadband makes online shopping inconvenient.
details: She usually makes a written grocery list and checks it against the amount set aside for food.
She buys store brands and compares unit prices rather than assuming the larger package is a better deal.
She is willing to use coupons when they apply to something she already buys, but will not travel across town to chase a small discount.
She buys clothes infrequently, often choosing basic secondhand items or waiting until a garment is genuinely worn out.
She does not shop for entertainment and feels uncomfortable when an outing is designed around spending.
She keeps a small list of household needs on the refrigerator so she can combine errands.
She will pay more for a durable, repairable item if she has seen it last, but does not trust marketing claims by themselves.
She avoids buy-now-pay-later offers and is cautious about store credit after earlier debt difficulties.
She prefers paying with a debit card or cash envelope and checks receipts when money is tight.
She delays replacing her phone and other electronics until the existing device becomes unreliable.

health_consciousness.pattern: She strongly values preventive health and tries to make practical choices about movement, nutrition, sleep, and stress. Her intentions are more consistent than her routine because household income, caregiving, disrupted sleep, and limited time narrow her options.
details: She keeps primary-care and dental appointments when she can arrange transportation and understand the likely cost.
She tries to take a daily walk, even if some days it is only a short loop to the corner store and back.
She watches her blood pressure and is willing to discuss preventive care with her clinician.
She wants regular meals but often eats late or relies on a convenient staple when work or caregiving disrupts the day.
She uses counseling as a practical resource rather than treating it as a sign that she has failed to cope.
She makes an effort to limit caffeine after the morning because it can worsen her sleep.
She is health-focused but does not expect herself to follow expensive diets, exercise programs, or wellness trends.

attitude_toward_new_products_and_technol.pattern: She is strongly skeptical of new consumer products and adopts them only when an existing item fails or a trusted person has a clear reason for recommending a replacement. She is particularly wary of connected devices, subscriptions, and products that collect personal data.
details: She does not want a smart speaker or a household device that listens for commands.
She keeps an older smartphone and uses only the functions she understands, such as calls, messages, maps, and basic email.
She can use work spreadsheets, grant portals, and standard office software, but has little patience for frequent interface changes.
She uses an employer-issued laptop for necessary work and does not treat it as a personal entertainment device.
Her home broadband is inconsistent; she sometimes completes sensitive work at the office rather than risk losing a connection.
She is more comfortable with a printed notice, paper form, or a person on the phone than a complicated self-service platform.
She researches safety and cost when replacing an essential item, but does not enjoy browsing product reviews.
She is not an early adopter and sometimes keeps a perfectly functional item longer than is convenient.

cultural_influences.pattern: Her cultural life is mostly local and community-based, shaped by a Catholic family and parish rather than by a strong claim to a single national tradition. Her family has Irish-American and French-Canadian ancestry, but she identifies plainly as a White, non-Hispanic American and does not treat ancestry as a credential.
details: She attends Mass most weeks when family and work obligations allow, and values the familiar faces as much as the service.
She participates in parish food drives and community meals, usually in practical supporting roles rather than as an organizer.
She keeps a few family holiday customs, including a quiet Christmas Eve gathering and calling relatives on major occasions.
She is uncomfortable when religious identity is used to shame people or settle questions that she believes belong to their own conscience.
Work travel has exposed her to different neighborhoods and clinic communities, but she is more a listener than a self-described cultural explorer.
Her strongest sense of belonging comes from long-standing local relationships, family stories, and community service.

travel_habits.pattern: She travels frequently enough for work that regional trips feel routine, but has little energy or money left for leisure exploration. Her work travel is mostly within the Northeast, and she is cautious about complicated itineraries.
details: She visits partner clinics two or three times in a typical month, commonly by employer-reimbursed mileage or a shared rental car.
She prefers a direct route, a printed address, and enough schedule margin to manage traffic rather than relying on last-minute navigation changes.
She sometimes combines two work stops in one trip to avoid wasting time and reimbursement funds.
Overnight travel is occasional and tiring; she prefers a modest hotel with a quiet room and a predictable check-in process.
She rarely takes international trips and has not had a substantial leisure vacation in many years.
For a personal outing she would choose a nearby beach, historic town, or state park over a complex multi-city itinerary.
She dislikes travel marketed as spontaneous adventure when it requires expensive bookings and uncertain transportation.

lifestyle.pattern: She prefers a modest, minimalist household with few possessions, not as a luxury aesthetic but because space, money, and energy are limited. She values flexibility, repair, and reduced waste, while recognizing that some of her frugality is imposed by circumstance.
details: She keeps only a small number of kitchen tools and uses the same dependable pans for years.
Her apartment is functional and lived-in rather than carefully decorated.
She owns a limited wardrobe in familiar colors and avoids clothes that require special care.
She reuses containers and bags, partly to save money and partly because throwing away something useful bothers her.
She likes having a clear surface to work at, but does not keep every part of the apartment perfectly orderly.
She is more comfortable walking or using a bus for local errands than owning multiple vehicles or making every outing a production.
She wants a simpler life but does not romanticize hardship; she would gladly accept more financial room and a reliable household appliance.

traits: Emotionally steady in a crisis: she can keep functioning when a family member is ill or a work deadline is approaching, even if she feels tired afterward.
Resilient without being invulnerable; she recovers from setbacks but remembers who left her to deal with the consequences.
Protective of people she considers overlooked, especially patients, low-wage workers, caregivers, and neighbors who have difficulty navigating institutions.
Deeply skeptical of powerful organizations and inclined to assume that polished public explanations leave out someone's financial interest.
Stubborn once she has settled on a political interpretation, and more likely than she should be to dismiss information that conflicts with it.
Practical and resourceful about money, transportation, meals, and making household items last.
Socially warm in a small group but not drawn to being the center of a large gathering.
Reliable with serious obligations; she keeps calendars, grant records, and appointments carefully even when other parts of the apartment are untidy.
Private about her own disappointments and reluctant to ask for help until the problem has become difficult to hide.
Compassionate in direct, personal encounters, but capable of being harsh in her judgments of people she sees as exploitative or self-serving.
Dryly funny, with a preference for understated observations over loud jokes.
Attached to familiar routines and inclined to regard unfamiliar products, platforms, and institutional changes as risks rather than conveniences.
Able to listen patiently when someone describes a personal problem, but less patient when a conversation becomes abstract or performative.
Proud of her professional competence and sensitive to being treated as a low-level clerical worker when she is actually carrying substantial responsibility.
More hopeful about local relationships than national politics; she believes a small group of people can solve concrete problems even when she is pessimistic about institutions.

big_five.openness: Low to moderate. Kathleen enjoys books, personal stories, and ideas about how communities work, but she is resistant to unfamiliar products, new technologies, and political arguments that challenge her established suspicions. She is more open to a new practice when it is introduced by someone she trusts and she can see how it works in everyday life.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderately high. She is diligent and accurate with grant records, work deadlines, bills, and medical appointments. Her organization is strongest where other people depend on her; household chores and personal projects can be postponed when caregiving or work becomes demanding.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate-low. She values regular contact with a few close friends, parish acquaintances, and family members, but large events and constant networking wear her out. She can speak up firmly in a meeting when she thinks an important point is being ignored.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate. She is kind and dependable in one-to-one relationships and will quietly help someone who needs practical support. She is less conciliatory about institutions, politicians, or people she believes are taking advantage of others, and can sound severe when arguing.
big_five.neuroticism: Low to moderate. She is generally emotionally regulated and does not panic easily, though sustained financial strain and disrupted sleep make her more irritable and rigid. She tends to manage worry by planning, seeking practical help, and talking with a counselor rather than displaying distress openly.

beliefs: Kathleen is strongly anti-capitalist. She believes that concentrated private ownership gives a small number of people too much control over work, housing, healthcare, and basic services.
She favors worker-owned cooperatives, community ownership, and public or accountable local provision of essential services over treating every necessity as a source of private profit.
She believes people who do the work should have a meaningful say in how workplaces are run and how the gains from their work are distributed.
She is especially hostile to private equity firms and large corporate landlords, which she sees as extracting money from communities without being answerable to the people who live there.

She supports regulation that protects workers, patients, and the environment, but is suspicious of complicated rules that small organizations must obey while large companies can hire specialists to navigate them.
She thinks many official rules are written or applied in ways that protect established institutions and make ordinary people feel powerless.
She is populist and anti-establishment: she wants people with ordinary jobs and ordinary bills to have more direct influence over public decisions.
She distrusts both major political parties and is registered as an unaffiliated voter; she believes party leaders often speak about working people more readily than they listen to them.
She does not believe that national institutions are neutral simply because they describe themselves as professional or independent.

She is not at all confident that elections are fair. Her distrust centers on opaque campaign money, district boundaries, inaccessible procedures, and weak public accountability rather than on one specific claim about a particular result.
Despite that distrust, she continues to vote in local and national elections because she sees participation as useful and does not want decisions made entirely by people with more money and time.
She believes democratic life is seriously threatened when neighbors stop believing that institutions can be questioned or held accountable.
She sees the state of moral values as a very big problem, but by moral values she means honesty, mutual obligation, respect, and whether people with power feel any duty toward those with less power.
She does not equate moral seriousness with restricting other people's private choices; to her, compassion and fairness are moral commitments too.
She believes abortion should be legal in all cases, and that a pregnant person should not have to satisfy a politician, judge, or religious authority before making a decision.
Her support for legal abortion is compatible with her Catholic identity because she treats religious teachings as matters of personal faith, not a basis for coercing people who do not share them.
She believes healthcare should be a dependable public responsibility and that people should not have to postpone basic care because they cannot predict the bill.
She considers healthcare affordability a serious problem, including for people who technically have insurance but still face deductibles, medication costs, and confusing coverage.
She believes addiction is a health and community problem that requires treatment, stable housing, and support, not only punishment.
She thinks inflation has caused her family severe hardship and notices rising prices most sharply in rent, groceries, transportation, and medical expenses.
She rates the economy as not so good even when official explanations describe positive overall figures, because those figures do not match the financial pressure she sees around her.
She feels her family's financial situation is worse than it was four years ago and is frustrated by being told that improvement is obvious when her own choices have narrowed.
She believes wage earners and caregivers are asked to absorb too much uncertainty while employers and institutions protect their own budgets first.
She supports public healthcare programs and would prefer a simpler system in which people do not have to repeatedly prove that they deserve care.
She favors practical gun-safety measures such as closing gaps in background checks, red-flag processes with due process, and better access to mental-health care.

She believes immigration policy should offer a workable path to legal status for people who are already contributing to their communities, while also expecting the government to maintain an orderly process.
She is wary of political arguments that blame immigrants for problems she believes are more directly connected to employers, housing shortages, and underfunded services.
She thinks climate and environmental risks should be handled honestly, but is suspicious when corporations use environmental language to sell products without changing their underlying practices.
She has little confidence in the Supreme Court as an institution and believes its members are too distant from the everyday consequences of their decisions.
She thinks partisan cooperation would improve public life, but does not believe cooperation should mean pretending that competing interests are the same.
Her Christian faith is important to her, though she disagrees with some church leaders and does not consider every religious authority beyond criticism.
She values parish community, ritual, and service more than public displays of piety or arguments over who counts as a proper Christian.
She believes people should be judged more by whether they keep their word and help others than by their income, job title, or political vocabulary.
She thinks new products are often introduced to create new spending or data collection rather than to solve a genuine problem.
She believes that a familiar, repairable product is usually preferable to a more advanced one if the advanced version adds cost, subscriptions, or privacy risks.
She believes preventive health matters but also thinks it is unfair to moralize about individual diets when people have limited money, time, or access to fresh food.
She believes close relationships are maintained through ordinary acts of reliability, not expensive gifts or constant online contact.
She sees local traditions as valuable when they create belonging and practical mutual support, but not when they are used to exclude newcomers or police private behavior.
She believes travel can broaden a person's understanding, but does not consider frequent business travel to be a substitute for rest or meaningful leisure.
She thinks a simple life can be satisfying, but does not confuse having few possessions because of financial constraint with freely chosen abundance.
skills: She has strong practical knowledge of grant administration, budget documentation, reporting deadlines, and audit preparation.
She can read a dense funding requirement and summarize the action items for a clinic manager in plain language.
She notices inconsistencies in receipts, dates, totals, and approval records without assuming that every mistake is deliberate.
She is skilled at keeping a meeting focused on decisions and recording who is responsible for the next step.
She knows how to approach local social-service offices, clinics, and nonprofit staff to find the right person to contact.
She can manage a household budget with a very small margin, including prioritizing rent, utilities, medication, food, and transportation.
She is competent with spreadsheets, word processing, email, and the grant portals required for work, but does not have broad digital troubleshooting skills.
She can travel independently around the Northeast for work and is good at planning routes with a reasonable buffer.
She has a good memory for names, relationships, and the history behind a workplace issue.
She is a patient listener when someone needs to explain a personal difficulty, though she may move quickly toward practical next steps.
She is comfortable facilitating a small discussion or training but does not enjoy public speaking to a large audience.
She knows how to stretch inexpensive ingredients into simple meals, even if she has little enthusiasm for elaborate cooking.

relationships.name: Daniel Dwyer
relationships.description: Daniel has a chronic back injury and currently has no wage income while he recovers and waits for a benefits decision. Their marriage is affectionate and long-standing but under pressure from money, pain, and the amount of caregiving Kathleen provides. He remains able to do some tasks on better days, and she tries to ask rather than automatically take over.

relationships.name: Rachel Dwyer
relationships.description: Rachel lives outside the household and works in a steady but modestly paid job. She checks in regularly and can help with occasional errands, though Kathleen avoids leaning on her financially and does not want every conversation to become a discussion about family problems.

relationships.name: Matthew Dwyer
relationships.description: Matthew lives independently and is less consistent about calling than his sister. Kathleen loves him and sometimes feels he does not appreciate how much planning a family crisis requires; they are closest when they are doing something practical together rather than arguing over politics.

relationships.name: Eileen Dwyer
relationships.description: Eileen lives in Pawtucket, a short trip away. Kathleen helps with occasional appointments and errands, but her mother remains mostly independent. Their conversations can be affectionate and frank, and they share family memories and a familiar religious background.

relationships.name: Gloria Santos
relationships.description: Gloria is a parish acquaintance who has become one of Kathleen's most dependable friends. She can disagree without turning every conversation into a test of loyalty and sometimes brings a meal or gives Kathleen a ride when work travel and caregiving collide.

relationships.name: Marisol Vega
relationships.description: Marisol manages the grants team and negotiated Kathleen's reduced-hours arrangement. She trusts Kathleen's judgment and is supportive, but also has to keep the network's deadlines and staffing needs in view. Kathleen respects her competence and is wary of promises about future promotions until they are put in writing.

relationships.name: Janet Kim
relationships.description: Janet coordinates clinic-level reporting and frequently needs Kathleen's help interpreting grant requirements. They work well together because Janet sends clear records and Kathleen explains what needs fixing without making a mistake feel like a personal failure.

relationships.name: Father Michael O'Leary
relationships.description: Kathleen respects his pastoral work and the parish's community programs, though she does not agree with every public statement made by church leaders. Their relationship is cordial and practical rather than one in which she seeks permission for personal decisions.

relationships.name: Renee Parker
relationships.description: Renee has helped Kathleen talk through caregiving stress, boundaries, and the difference between what she can influence and what she cannot. Kathleen appreciates that Renee does not dismiss her concerns or simply tell her to be more positive.

occupation.title: Not employed; preschool-age child
occupation.organization: No employer. She attends a local Head Start program as a young child.
occupation.description: Lillian is three and is not expected to participate in the labor force. She is financially and practically dependent on her mother and maternal grandmother. Her household has an annual cash income below $25,000, earned mainly through her mother's variable part-time work, and relies on public benefits and careful budgeting for essentials. Lillian's ordinary responsibilities are age-appropriate: putting a few toys in a bin, bringing her shoes to the door, and trying to wash her hands with an adult's help. These are learning routines, not work.

interests: Picture books about animals, especially dogs, cats, ducks, and farm animals.
Stories with repetition, predictable phrases, and a chance to point out objects on the page.
Pretend grocery-store play using empty food packages and a little basket.
Playing family or kitchen with dolls, plastic dishes, and a blanket for a bed.
Building short towers with large blocks and knocking them down.
Duplo-style blocks and chunky puzzles with a few familiar pieces.
Drawing circles, lines, and large loops with washable crayons.
Stickers, particularly animals and bright shapes, though she sometimes puts them somewhere unexpected.
Bubbles and watching them drift, pop, or stick briefly to the pavement.
Sidewalk chalk, especially making marks and asking an adult what they look like.
Water play at the sink or in a shallow basin with close adult supervision.
The playground slide, after checking that a familiar person is nearby.
Short walks where she can stop and look at leaves, dogs, buses, and construction equipment.
Singing familiar nursery songs and making up a few words of her own.
Dancing to upbeat music in the living room, particularly when an adult joins in.
Simple matching games and puzzles when she is not expected to sit for too long.
Looking at family photographs and hearing the names of relatives.
Helping stir pancake batter or wash a piece of fruit with an adult beside her.
Watching the bus arrive and leave from a safe place with her grandmother.
Playing with a soft toy dog that she carries around the apartment.
Pretend doctor play, usually with a toy stethoscope or a bandage for a doll.
Helping put napkins on the table, mainly because it makes her feel included.
Watching short children's programs with songs, clear characters, and gentle humor.
Imagining that the couch is a boat or that a laundry basket is a car.
likes: Being read to while sitting close to her mother or grandmother.
Choosing between two outfits, even when she then changes her mind.
The blue handled cup she recognizes as hers.
Warm grits, pancakes, and oatmeal when they are not too hot.
Banana slices, applesauce, strawberries when available, and canned peaches.
Chicken, scrambled eggs, macaroni and cheese, and soft rice.
Mild flavors and familiar foods served separately rather than mixed together.
A small cookie as an occasional treat, especially if it is offered with a familiar routine.
The sound of rain from indoors, though she dislikes getting soaked unexpectedly.
Watching a ceiling fan or a spinning playground wheel for a few seconds.
Dogs that are calm and kept on a leash.
Being praised for trying, even when a task is not finished neatly.
A heads-up before leaving a fun activity.
Having a familiar adult sit nearby while she starts playing with another child.
Soft pajamas, her small blanket, and the same bedtime story on difficult nights.
Bright colors, particularly yellow, blue, and pink, without a rigid preference.
Music that lets her clap, stomp, or copy an easy movement.
A short trip on the bus when she gets a window seat beside her grandmother.
Playing outside in mild weather with chalk or a ball.
Having a grown-up describe what is happening instead of hurrying her through it.
A new toy or snack if someone she trusts first shows her how it works.
Pretending to help with real household tasks using child-safe objects.
dislikes: Being rushed while she is trying to put on shoes or a coat.
A sudden goodbye without time to understand that her caregiver is leaving.
Loud hand dryers, blenders, and unexpected alarms.
Strongly spicy food, bitter tastes, and unfamiliar sauces touching foods she already likes.
Food that is too hot, too cold, or has an unexpected texture.
Having a favored toy taken without warning.
Waiting while adults have a long conversation and do not explain what is happening.
A crowded room where she cannot easily find her caregiver.
Scratchy clothing tags, stiff shoes, and wet socks.
Hair detangling when she is already tired; she prefers a warning and a gentle pace.
Being told she is a 'big girl' as a reason she should not need comfort.
A long car ride without a break or something familiar to look at.
An unfamiliar adult asking her many questions at once.
Having to stop playing without a clear next step.
People laughing when she makes a mistake, even if they mean it kindly.
A television program with loud conflict or frightening characters.
Bathwater being poured over her head unexpectedly.
Sharing a snack before she has had time to understand that there is enough for everyone.
Being corrected repeatedly while she is still trying to express a thought.
Being left in a new setting before she has had a chance to look around.
preferences.culinary_tastes: Lillian eats an ordinary omnivorous preschool diet and has no stated family rule against meat or animal products. Her familiar foods lean toward mild, simple meals: eggs, chicken, rice, grits, pasta, cooked vegetables, fruit, and occasional cookies. She is not reliably adventurous with food; she may inspect or sniff a new item before tasting it, and often accepts it more readily when a caregiver eats some first. Household meals mix Southern family favorites with inexpensive convenience foods, depending on time and money. She has no independent understanding of nutrition, organic labels, or food shopping.
preferences.shopping_habits: She does not shop independently or understand prices, budgets, or online purchasing. Her mother and grandmother make occasional, planned grocery and discount-store trips, usually prioritizing food, laundry supplies, clothing, and household necessities. Lillian may accompany them and ask for a snack or colorful item after seeing it, but those requests are not treated as decisions. She enjoys helping choose between two practical options, such as which fruit to put in the basket, and can become restless during a long errand. Online orders are an adult convenience rather than a child interest.
preferences.health_consciousness: Lillian has no developed health ideology and does not choose foods or activities on the basis of wellness claims. Her caregivers try to offer water, regular meals, outdoor play, sleep routines, and ordinary medical care, while the realities of cost, work schedules, weather, and fatigue sometimes make routines uneven. She likes active play when it is available but also spends quiet time with books and toys. Adults, not Lillian, decide about medical appointments, medication, food safety, and screen limits.
preferences.attitude_toward_new_products: She is curious about bright, tactile objects but cautious about unfamiliar foods, noisy toys, or anything that changes a familiar routine. A trusted adult demonstrating a product and allowing her to touch it at her own pace usually helps. She does not evaluate brands or make purchase decisions; novelty matters to her mainly as a chance to explore, imitate, or play.
preferences.cultural_influences: Her everyday cultural world is mostly local and family-centered: Memphis streets, familiar relatives, neighborhood shops, children's books, Head Start routines, and songs heard at home or church. She is also exposed to nationally popular children's shows, music, and toys through family and preschool. Her caregivers value family gatherings and Southern food traditions but do not make her perform a polished version of regional identity. She hears occasional Spanish words at preschool but speaks English at home and does not yet have a sophisticated understanding of cultural differences.
preferences.travel_habits: Lillian is a home-oriented preschooler whose usual journeys are local: Head Start, a grocery store, a nearby playground, a clinic, or a relative's home. The household has limited transportation flexibility, so adults plan around a bus route, rides from family, or the occasional borrowed car. She has not independently traveled or taken international trips. She enjoys seeing buses and unfamiliar neighborhoods but needs predictable meals, bathroom access, and a familiar adult on longer outings.
preferences.lifestyle: Her life is urban and modest, centered on a rented home, family care, preschool, neighborhood errands, and low-cost play. She is neither a deliberately minimalist nor an extravagant consumer; most toys are modest, reused, or received from relatives. She alternates between energetic outdoor play and sedentary activities such as looking at books, drawing, or watching a short program. Her daily routine is shaped more by caregiver work shifts, transport, weather, and household resources than by a highly scheduled enrichment calendar.

personality.developmental_note: These are descriptions of current, changeable preschool behavior, not fixed adult character judgments. Her behavior is strongly affected by sleep, hunger, transitions, noise, and whether a trusted caregiver is present.
traits: Curious about small details; she will stop to inspect a beetle, a crack in the sidewalk, or the sound a cupboard makes.
Cautious at first in unfamiliar places, especially if adults leave quickly, but more willing to join once she has watched for a while.
Affectionate with familiar people and apt to lean against her mother or grandmother while listening to a story.
Determined about small choices, sometimes insisting on the same cup or on putting on a shoe herself even when it takes several tries.
Playful and imaginative, especially when turning ordinary household items into pretend food, a bus, or a doctor's kit.
Sensitive to abrupt changes; a warning before leaving the playground often helps, though it does not prevent every protest.
Socially interested but not consistently comfortable sharing a favored toy; she is still learning how to wait and trade.
Quick to notice adult emotion and may ask 'you okay?' if someone looks upset, without fully understanding the reason.
Easily delighted by physical comedy, bubbles, animal sounds, and familiar songs.
Prone to strong, short-lived feelings: frustration can become a tantrum and then pass once she is comforted or redirected.
Proud of tasks she can do herself and likely to repeat 'I did it' until someone acknowledges her effort.
More cooperative when offered two acceptable choices than when given a broad instruction with no context.
Comfort-seeking when tired, sometimes carrying a small blanket or asking for the same bedtime book.
Not consistently patient; waiting is difficult when she can see a snack or a desired toy.
Resilient in the ordinary preschool sense: after a hard moment, she often returns to play when an adult helps her settle.

big_five.openness: Moderate to high in play and sensory exploration. She enjoys pretend scenarios, new playground equipment, and unfamiliar picture books when a trusted adult introduces them, but can be wary of unfamiliar foods, loud characters, or abrupt changes.
big_five.conscientiousness: Not meaningfully comparable to adult conscientiousness. She sometimes follows familiar routines and likes completing simple tasks, but needs reminders, supervision, and help with transitions.
big_five.extraversion: Moderate and context-dependent. She is lively and chatty with family and familiar classmates, while in a new setting she may stay beside an adult and observe before approaching others.
big_five.agreeableness: Emerging and variable. She can be affectionate, helpful, and eager to please, but normal preschool possessiveness and frustration make sharing or stopping an enjoyable activity difficult.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderate, expressed as sensitivity to fatigue, separation, noise, and disrupted routines rather than as adult-style worry. She usually settles with reassurance, a predictable next step, and a familiar caregiver.

beliefs: Her understanding of the world is concrete, still developing, and often based on what she has just seen; these are not adult-like convictions.
She expects her mother or grandmother to return after a familiar goodbye, though separation can still make her upset.
She treats the apartment as a safe home base where familiar people, blankets, and toys should be findable.
She sometimes behaves as though a stuffed dog can understand her pretend conversations.
She knows that real dogs are animals but may need a reminder not to approach an unfamiliar one without an adult.
She expects meals and snacks to appear through adult care and does not understand the household budget behind them.
She has learned that some foods are for breakfast and some are for dinner, though the categories are flexible.
She thinks a food can be 'yucky' before tasting it if its appearance or smell seems unfamiliar.
She has a growing sense that a short wait may end with a snack, a turn, or a caregiver's return, but her sense of time is limited.
She understands that some household objects are off limits because an adult says they may be hot, sharp, or unsafe.
She sometimes believes that saying 'please' can help an adult agree, but is still learning that it does not guarantee a yes.
She recognizes that a teacher has a role in the classroom and that her mother or grandmother comes to pick her up.
She expects songs and favorite books to repeat in the same way and may correct an adult who skips a familiar line.
She is beginning to understand that another child can want the same toy she wants, although sharing remains difficult in the moment.
She may think an adult's brief absence means they are in another room rather than understanding work, money, or schedules.
She knows that rain makes the ground wet and sometimes expects puddles after a storm.
She enjoys cause and effect, such as dropping a block and hearing it land, and may repeat the action to check what happens.
She believes that small acts of pretend play can change the meaning of an object: a basket can become a car or a bed for a doll.
She notices when an adult is sad or cross and may assume she caused it unless the adult reassures her.
She has an emerging idea that some things belong to her and some belong to others, but ownership is not yet consistently applied during play.
She expects familiar routines such as washing hands before some meals, though reminders are still needed.
She knows that Head Start is a place where she plays, eats, listens to stories, and sees children and teachers.
She is starting to understand that some adults go to work while she is at school, without knowing much about their jobs or wages.
She has no developed opinion about household income, shopping strategy, online commerce, or the difference between expensive and inexpensive goods.
She tends to trust familiar caregivers' demonstrations of unfamiliar toys and foods more than an unfamiliar person's explanation.
She shows a preference for mild flavors and familiar textures, but this is a sensory and learning preference rather than a moral view of food.
She has no settled understanding of organic food, health claims, or why adults sometimes choose one product over another.
She has no meaningful political opinions about government, elections, immigration, public policy, or the economy.
She has no settled religious doctrine; she may recognize a familiar song or gathering at church as something adults do together.
She has not formed adult views about travel, culture, social class, or whether urban or rural life is preferable.
She behaves more confidently when an adult explains what comes next and offers a small choice, suggesting that predictability currently feels reassuring.
skills: Uses short phrases to ask for familiar people, foods, toys, help, or a turn.
Recognizes a few familiar adults and classmates by name and face.
Can follow simple one- and two-step directions when she is calm and paying attention.
Can point to common body parts, household objects, and animals in pictures.
Uses a spoon and open cup with some spills; adults still supervise meals.
Can remove some simple clothing items and is learning to put on shoes and a coat.
Participates in handwashing and tidying when an adult demonstrates each step.
Can stack blocks, turn pages, make crayon marks, and complete simple inset puzzles.
Uses pretend play to imitate routines such as cooking, shopping, or caring for a doll.
Can indicate some basic needs, though she may not explain a complicated feeling before becoming upset.
Has beginning turn-taking skills when an adult helps structure the game.
Is learning to pedal and steer a small tricycle, with a helmet and close supervision.
Can remember a familiar song's refrain and join in with gestures.
Has no professional, technical, financial, research, or independent consumer expertise; her abilities are normal early-childhood skills.

relationships.name: Renee Parker
relationships.description: Lillian's primary caregiver. Renee works variable part-time shifts in hotel housekeeping and is often tired, but tries to keep preschool, meals, and bedtime reasonably predictable. She is affectionate and attentive, though money and schedule pressures sometimes make her short-tempered. Lillian seeks her out for comfort and watches her face to gauge whether a request is likely to be accepted.

relationships.name: Denise Parker
relationships.description: Shares the rented home with Renee and Lillian and provides much of the childcare around Renee's shifts. Denise is patient about play and stories but firm about traffic, hot pans, and other safety rules. Lillian calls her 'Nana' and is especially comfortable sitting beside her during breakfast or looking through family photographs.

relationships.name: Marcus Hill
relationships.description: Lives elsewhere in the Memphis area and has intermittent contact with Lillian. He sometimes visits or speaks with her by phone, but the schedule is not dependable enough for her to anticipate it without adult preparation. Lillian knows him as her father but is too young to understand the adults' arrangements or their financial and personal disagreements.

relationships.name: Ms. Carla
relationships.description: A familiar teacher who greets Lillian by name and helps her enter classroom activities gradually. Lillian is more comfortable when Ms. Carla explains a change before it happens and gives her a specific job, such as carrying the book basket.

relationships.name: Ava
relationships.description: A familiar preschool playmate. Lillian likes sitting near Ava during songs and copying her pretend play, but they occasionally both want the same toy and need a teacher's help to take turns.

relationships.name: Tasha Parker
relationships.description: Visits when her work and transport allow, sometimes bringing hand-me-down clothes or a book. Lillian is fond of her but may need a few minutes to warm up if they have not seen each other recently.

occupation.title: Part-time apartment maintenance worker and occasional event setup worker
occupation.organization: A locally owned apartment complex in Albuquerque, with occasional shifts through a small event-rental company
occupation.employment_status: Employed part time, usually between 24 and 30 hours a week at the apartment complex, with irregular weekend or seasonal event shifts when work is available.
occupation.description: Curtis handles basic repairs and upkeep at a mid-sized apartment complex. He changes light fixtures, patches small holes, replaces faucet washers, clears walkways, moves supplies, checks common areas, and lets licensed contractors know when a problem is beyond his ability or authorization. He knows the property and its long-term tenants well and is often the person residents approach when a door sticks or a smoke alarm chirps. He likes being useful and dislikes sitting indoors for a whole shift. His hours are limited by the property’s budget rather than by a lack of willingness to work. He sometimes earns extra money helping an event-rental crew load tables, chairs, and canopies, though those shifts are inconsistent and physically tiring. His total gross household income is approximately $34,600 in a typical year; he lives alone, so there is no second household earner. The work provides no dependable health insurance, paid leave, or guaranteed schedule. He is proud of knowing how to fix practical problems but resents being expected to perform skilled work at entry-level pay.

interests: Short domestic trips by car or public transportation, especially to see family or visit a place he can explore on foot.
Caring for his senior cat, including talking to her while he prepares food and checking that she is comfortable.
Walking briskly through neighborhood streets, parks, and commercial areas rather than treating exercise as a formal gym activity.
Watching car-repair demonstrations and practical how-to videos on his phone.
Trying new phone features, inexpensive gadgets, work gloves, flashlights, and compact tools.
Talking with tenants and familiar shopkeepers, even when he has no particular errand.
Watching local news and national political commentary, sometimes more often than is good for his mood.
Listening to classic rock, country, and oldies while driving or doing small jobs.
Following family updates and photos through text messages and social media.
Browsing discount stores, hardware aisles, and online listings for a tool or device that might solve a practical problem.
likes: Vegetable-heavy meals with beans, rice, greens, squash, tomatoes, onions, and whatever produce is affordable that week.
Pinto beans and rice prepared with a little chile, garlic, and cumin.
Green chile when it is available, though he prefers manageable heat rather than a meal that becomes a test of endurance.
Oatmeal, bananas, apples, and peanut butter as inexpensive foods he can keep at home.
A good breakfast burrito as an occasional treat, especially after an early shift.
Homemade vegetable soup that can be reheated for several days.
A diner with counter seating, straightforward portions, and staff who remember regular customers.
Coffee in the morning, usually plain or with a little creamer; he is not interested in elaborate coffee rituals.
Comfortable walking shoes with a sturdy sole, even if they are not fashionable.
A clean, working tool that fits his hand and does not require a complicated app.
Simple explanations that let him decide for himself rather than pressuring him to agree.
A phone with a responsive screen, a long battery life, and useful camera and map functions.
Getting a new product in his hands, testing its basic functions, and figuring out its quirks.
Neighborhood parks with benches, shade, and paths that do not require a fee.
Driving on a clear day with the windows partly open and music playing at a comfortable volume.
Local markets and small shops where he can ask a person a question instead of searching through a complicated website.
Animals that approach him without being coaxed; he enjoys quietly earning a pet’s trust.
His granddaughter showing him a drawing, a game, or a small discovery she is excited about.
Old photographs and stories about people in his family, even though he does not feel strongly tied to a particular ancestral tradition.
A practical favor returned without keeping score, such as someone bringing in a package or lending a socket wrench.
A familiar church service on the occasions when he attends, especially the music and the chance to greet people afterward.
Short walks after dinner that help him wind down without requiring gym membership or specialized equipment.
Secondhand tools and household items that still work well and cost less than new ones.
Being thanked for noticing and fixing a small problem before it becomes a larger one.
A modest motel or clean budget lodging on a trip, where he can park easily and sleep without fuss.
dislikes: Being told that financial hardship is simply a result of laziness or poor character.
Being treated as though a high school education means he cannot understand a complicated issue.
Automated customer-service menus that repeat the same options without connecting him to a person.
Unexpected fees, subscription renewals, and purchases that quietly convert into recurring charges.
Expensive restaurants where he cannot tell whether the menu will suit his tastes or his budget.
Wasteful packaging and products that look sturdy online but feel flimsy when delivered.
People who interrupt him and then accuse him of being the one who will not listen.
Long, crowded indoor events where he cannot easily step outside for air.
Overly sweet snacks when he is looking for something filling rather than dessert.
Salads sold as a complete meal when they are mostly a few leaves and cost more than a hot plate of food.
Being pressured to adopt a new social or political vocabulary before anyone explains what they mean by it.
Mandatory app updates that move familiar buttons or make a device harder to use.
Having to sit still through a whole day when a walk or practical task would help him feel better.
People who make jokes about older adults being unable to use technology.
Political conversations framed as if everyone who disagrees is evil, stupid, or beyond discussion.
A damp, cluttered apartment and litter left near the building entrance.
Car repairs that are explained vaguely and priced without showing what is actually wrong.
Missing a family gathering because his schedule or transportation fell through.
Medical bills that arrive after he thought a visit was already paid for.
Being asked to take on unpaid work simply because he is handy.
Cold meals that have gone soggy during delivery.
A phone battery dying when he needs maps, transit information, or a way to reach family.
People who make promises casually and then disappear when it is time to follow through.
The feeling that a conversation has become a contest in which nobody is allowed to admit uncertainty.
A sharp, nagging ache in his knee that makes him shorten a walk he had been looking forward to.
shopping_and_product_tendencies: He checks prices and looks for discounts because his budget leaves little room for mistakes.
He buys groceries mostly in person so he can compare produce and avoid delivery fees, but he orders selected small items online when the price is clearly better.
He is an early adopter of consumer gadgets when a useful new model or feature catches his attention, though he is not an early adopter of every trend.
He occasionally makes an impulsive technology purchase and then compensates by cutting back on takeout or other small expenses.
He is more loyal to a product that has lasted through real use than to a brand’s claims or advertising.
He likes demonstrations and hands-on testing, and will ask a clerk direct questions if he does not understand a feature.
He tends to choose practical products in familiar colors and avoids paying extra for decorative versions.
culinary_and_health_preferences: His ordinary diet is centered on vegetables, grains, beans, and fruit, mainly because these foods can be filling and economical.
He is not strict about vegetarianism and may eat meat at a family gathering or order it when that is the simplest affordable option.
He prefers everyday food that is recognizable and satisfying over elaborate restaurant presentation.
He likes some chile and seasoning but generally wants enough flavor without extreme heat.
He enjoys cooking simple one-pot meals when he has time, but his work hours and finances sometimes push him toward convenience food.
He would like to make more health-focused choices, but access, price, time, and fatigue often matter more than intention.

traits: Outgoing and energetic; he usually enjoys being around people and can strike up conversation while waiting in line.
Strongly self-reliant, sometimes to the point of treating an offer of help as an implied judgment about his competence.
Persistent once he has decided that a task or position matters.
Rigid in several moral and political convictions and unusually resistant to evidence he considers hostile or manipulative.
Curious about new consumer technology and eager to try devices or product features before many of his friends do.
More cautious about broad social or cultural change than about a new phone, tool, or household gadget.
Practical and resourceful when dealing with repairs, transportation, and small household problems.
Sociable and often generous with time, particularly when an older tenant or animal needs help.
Proud, with a sensitive response to being corrected in public or treated as unintelligent.
Pessimistic about the national economy and his own prospects, but still capable of looking forward to a trip or a family visit.
Argumentative when he feels a core belief is being challenged, though not constantly hostile in everyday interactions.
Emotionally guarded about the divorce and financial strain; he uses humor or a political complaint to change the subject.
Protective toward his children and granddaughter, even when that protectiveness comes out as unsolicited advice.
Impatient with bureaucracy, long forms, automated phone menus, and explanations he feels are deliberately evasive.
Capable of loyalty and gratitude; he remembers who helped him during a difficult period and tries to repay favors.
Restless when he has been indoors too long and inclined to turn errands into a walk around the neighborhood.

big_five.openness: Low to moderate overall, but uneven. Curtis eagerly explores new phones, apps, small tools, and household products because he likes novelty he can test directly. He is far less open to ideas that challenge his settled moral, religious, or political judgments, and he tends to distrust cultural changes he believes are being imposed rather than chosen.
big_five.conscientiousness: Moderate. He is dependable about scheduled maintenance shifts and tasks affecting other people, but his personal paperwork, budgeting, and preventive appointments are often delayed. Irregular hours, financial pressure, and a tendency to act on immediate needs make long-range planning difficult.
big_five.extraversion: High. He gains energy from conversation, group activities, practical collaboration, and being recognized as useful. He can dominate a discussion when excited and has to make an effort to notice when a quieter person wants space.
big_five.agreeableness: Moderate to low in disagreement, moderate to high in practical acts of care. He can be helpful, neighborly, and funny, but stubbornness, blunt judgments, and suspicion of opposing motives make him difficult to persuade once he feels challenged.
big_five.neuroticism: Moderately high under pressure. Money worries, poor-quality sleep, uncertainty about elections, and fear of losing independence can make him irritable and ruminative. He is not distressed all the time; exercise, familiar company, and a concrete task usually settle him.

beliefs: Personal liberty should be the starting point for laws and public policy, and government should have to justify restrictions rather than assume people need to be managed.
Adults should generally be allowed to make private decisions without unnecessary government interference.
He values privacy and dislikes the idea of institutions collecting personal information without a clear reason.
He identifies as libertarian-leaning and usually sees himself as politically independent rather than loyal to a party.
He believes individual effort, persistence, useful skills, and prudent choices are major contributors to financial success.
He also recognizes that illness, rent, layoffs, and family responsibilities can overwhelm even a person who works hard, although he is reluctant to make structural explanations the whole story.
He believes people should be able to see plainly how their taxes are being used.
He is suspicious of large bureaucracies and assumes they often protect their own procedures before they help ordinary people.
He thinks people should be judged by what they do in their immediate lives more than by the political labels they use.
He is concerned about the possibility of post-election violence and thinks inflammatory political rhetoric can push unstable people toward real-world harm.
He is somewhat confident that elections are fair, but does not believe every official explanation deserves unquestioning trust.
He is wary of both major parties and will sometimes argue that neither one takes the daily costs faced by working people seriously.
He rates the economy as poor because prices, rent, and repair bills feel harder to manage than his income.
He believes his family’s financial position is worse than it was four years ago, even though some of the pressure comes from gradual changes rather than one dramatic event.
He describes inflation as a moderate hardship: he can usually cover the basics, but has to delay purchases and give up small comforts.
He believes a person can be compassionate without agreeing with every political program proposed in the name of compassion.
His Christian faith is sincere but personal; he values moral accountability, mercy, and humility more than denominational labels or elaborate religious argument.
He believes life is morally serious and that people should take responsibility for the consequences of their choices.

He believes abortion should be illegal in most cases because he views unborn life as morally significant; he finds this conviction more compelling than the libertarian argument in this particular issue and does not experience the two commitments as fully reconcilable.
He is more willing to discuss exceptions when a pregnancy threatens the mother’s life, but he remains opposed to treating abortion as an ordinary, consequence-free choice.
He believes people who disagree about abortion should still be spoken to as human beings rather than turned into targets for intimidation.
He thinks healthcare is too expensive and believes people should be able to find affordable treatment before a manageable problem becomes an emergency.
He nevertheless delays or avoids his own care when he expects a bill he cannot pay or fears being pushed into tests and follow-up appointments he cannot afford.
He believes useful skills deserve respect, whether or not the person who has them attended college.
He believes a fair wage should reflect the difficulty and responsibility of the work, not only the worker’s ability to negotiate.
He is skeptical of sweeping claims that one policy or one politician can fix a complex economic problem quickly.
He believes people should be allowed to try unfamiliar products and make their own choices about technology, while also believing companies should clearly disclose costs and privacy practices.
He is more open to new consumer products than to social changes he perceives as abrupt, compulsory, or dismissive of older norms.
He often feels that mainstream cultural categories do not describe him, and he is more comfortable building a personal identity from chosen interests and relationships.
He does not feel an obligation to reproduce the customs of his parents or grandparents just because they were inherited.
He believes family relationships require showing up, not only saying that family matters.
He thinks older relatives should offer advice only when they have earned enough trust to be heard, though he does not always follow that rule himself.
He believes exercise should be an ordinary part of life and not an expensive performance involving equipment, memberships, or special clothing.
He thinks animals deserve attentive care and should not be taken in casually by someone who cannot provide for them.
He believes a person should be able to take a short trip or enjoy a modest pleasure without being called irresponsible, even when that person is under financial pressure.
He dislikes public shaming and believes people usually change their minds more readily when they are treated with respect.
He is intensely suspicious of messages that ask him to accept a major change immediately and discourage questions; he may hold that suspicion even when the proposal is reasonable.

He can acknowledge uncertainty about practical details, but tends to treat disagreement with his core moral and political positions as evidence that the other person has not looked at the facts carefully.
He believes the strongest proof of a claim is whether it holds up in ordinary life, which sometimes helps him spot empty promises and sometimes leads him to discount evidence that is less visible.
skills: Can handle basic apartment maintenance, including minor plumbing repairs, replacing fixtures, patching drywall, and recognizing when a job requires a licensed contractor.
Comfortable using hand tools and common power tools safely for routine tasks.
Can troubleshoot simple problems with household appliances, locks, doors, and lighting.
Has practical experience loading and securing tables, chairs, and event equipment.
Knows basic car maintenance, including checking fluids, changing a tire, and identifying common warning signs, though he relies on a mechanic for major repairs.
Can navigate Albuquerque by familiar streets, bus routes, and smartphone maps.
Learns consumer technology quickly by experimenting, watching demonstrations, and exploring settings.
Uses texting, maps, online shopping, banking apps, and social media regularly, though he sometimes needs help with complicated forms or account recovery.
Can make inexpensive, filling meals from beans, rice, vegetables, eggs, and pantry staples.
Reads people well in informal settings and is good at getting a frustrated tenant to explain what is actually wrong.
Is comfortable speaking up to a property manager when a repair or schedule seems unreasonable.
Can keep working through a tiring shift and often takes pride in finishing a physical task.
Has an instinct for spotting small maintenance problems before they become costly.
Can tell a story in a lively, memorable way, especially about work, family, travel, or a repair that went wrong.
Is able to admit when a tool or task is beyond his training, especially when safety or property damage is at stake.

relationships.name: Denise Maddox
relationships.description: Curtis’s former wife, approximately 60. They divorced about fourteen years ago after a long period of accumulated disagreements rather than one single dramatic event. They are no longer a couple, but they can coordinate around their adult children and granddaughter. Curtis sometimes speaks defensively about the marriage and still feels that his efforts were not recognized; he does not want Denise harmed and can cooperate when a family need requires it.

relationships.name: Melissa Maddox
relationships.description: His daughter, 34, who lives elsewhere in the Albuquerque area and works full time. They care about each other, but she has learned to limit conversations that become lectures about politics or decisions he thinks she should make. Curtis wants to be included in her life and sometimes struggles to show that interest without immediately offering advice.

relationships.name: Brian Maddox
relationships.description: His son, 30, who lives in another New Mexico city. Their relationship is affectionate but intermittently distant. They share practical interests such as cars and household repairs, which give them an easier route into conversation than discussing the divorce or Curtis’s finances.

relationships.name: Lila
relationships.description: His granddaughter, 7. Curtis enjoys taking her to a park, bringing her a small inexpensive treat, and listening to her explain what she is drawing or watching. He tries to be a playful grandfather, although he occasionally has to be reminded not to turn a simple visit into a lesson.

relationships.name: Manny Ortega
relationships.description: A long-time coworker in the apartment complex’s maintenance operation, in his early 50s. Manny is more patient with residents and has occasionally helped Curtis with a ride or a difficult repair. They joke and trade practical tips, but Manny will change the subject when Curtis starts a heated political monologue.

relationships.name: Ruth Alvarez
relationships.description: A neighbor in her late 60s who lives in the same building. They exchange small favors, talk in the courtyard, and sometimes share information about local services. Curtis checks whether she has received packages and she reminds him when he has left tools near a shared walkway.

relationships.name: Pastor Elaine Brooks
relationships.description: The pastor of a small Protestant congregation Curtis sometimes attends. She respects his faith without assuming he agrees with every church member or political position. Curtis appreciates that she is willing to speak plainly and listen, though he can become defensive if a sermon seems to challenge his moral judgments.

relationships.name: Moxie
relationships.description: Curtis’s senior gray tabby cat, around 11. Moxie is his only regular household companion, and he is attentive to her habits and appetite. Veterinary costs worry him, but he budgets for routine food and seeks low-cost care when he can.

occupation.title: Self-employed plumbing and heating contractor
occupation.organization: Keegan Mechanical Services, a small Providence-area repair and maintenance business
occupation.description: Martin owns and works in a small plumbing and heating service company. He handles diagnostic visits, estimates, difficult repairs, scheduling, supplier calls, customer complaints, and much of the paperwork. Two experienced technicians take on some scheduled work, but Martin still gets pulled into jobs when a boiler is behaving unpredictably or a customer wants the owner to explain a bill. His business serves older homes, small landlords, restaurants, and a few neighborhood commercial properties. He is good at identifying the likely cause of a problem before replacing parts and dislikes selling a costly replacement when a repair is safe and sensible. His workload and payments are uneven: some commercial invoices take weeks to clear, winter demand can be intense, and a few large jobs can make one year look much more prosperous than the next. His most recent full-year household income was about $214,000 before personal taxes, largely from the business, but that headline figure is not a dependable monthly paycheck. Taxes, insurance, a personally guaranteed business credit line, vehicle costs, medical expenses, and help for his mother absorb much of the money. His current cash flow is severely strained; he has little emergency savings, has carried balances on personal cards, and sometimes has to decide which essential bill can wait until a customer pays.

interests: Cooking an ordinary dinner from scratch when his schedule allows.
Baking bread or a simple loaf cake on an unusually quiet weekend.
Older houses and the practical history visible in their pipes, radiators, and patched-over renovations.
Watching a repair video when he needs to understand a particular fitting or unfamiliar appliance.
Local history, especially Providence neighborhoods and old mill buildings.
Listening to music from different countries after discovering it through a radio program or a friend's recommendation.
Following a few international soccer matches without treating himself as a devoted expert.
Reading newspaper articles, practical nonfiction, and the occasional crime novel.
Short neighborhood walks, especially when he can take a route past familiar houses.
Small repair projects at home, provided they do not turn into an expensive renovation.
Visiting a hardware or plumbing supply counter where the staff know the parts and will give a straight answer.
Having a quiet meal with his mother or sister rather than arranging a large family event.
likes: Food with a noticeable chili kick, smoky heat, or assertive garlic rather than food that is merely hot for show.
